speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. EDMOND PROULX (Prescott) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 77, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act. He said: This Bill is intended further to secure the independence of members of the Senate and House of Commons, and at the same time to safeguard the interests of the country. In these days of extensive purchases by the Government without public tender, I believe that the present legislation on this subject needs to be amended. As the law is at present, a member of this House or of the Senate is prevented from having any contract or business dealings with the Government, but he may be a shareholder in a company, and be largely interested in that company, which has the right to contract with the Government, except in the case of a company which undertakes to contract for a public building or other public work. By this Bill, I wish to add to the companies prevented from dealing with the government any company in which a member of this House or of the Senate is a director, or in which he holds, directly or indirectly, a controlling interest.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic
subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance), the House went into 
Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Bank Act by permitting the chartered banks up to the 1st day of July, 1915, to lend money for the purchase of seed grain upon the security of the grain purchased, the crop to be grown therefrom, and the grain threshed from the crop, and that any Act founded on this resolution be deemed to have come into force on the 15th day of March, 1915.

This resolution is almost self-explanatory. We propose to amend section 88 of the Bank Act by allowing a bank to lend money to the owner, tenant or occupier of land for the purchase of seed grain, upon the security of the crop to be grown from such seed grain. At present it is not open to the banks to take such security, and it was thought advisable, having regard to the desirability during this year of greatly increasing production and prevailing financial conditions, that the amendment should be made and this additional power given to the banks. Representations have been made to me for some time past with regard to this matter. I took it up with all the chartered banks in Canada, and while it appears perfectly clear from the replies which I have received from the banks that the general credit and standing of the borrower will still be a controlling factor in their determination of whether or not loans will be made, it would appear also that it may be an advantage to the borrowing community that this legislation should be enacted, as the banks would, I am convinced, be more ready to lend than if they were not permitted to take this security.

The present provisions of the Act covered this-not so far, I admit, as lending on the seed grain itself, which would be no security; but after that seed grain is once sown and harvested, the present provisions of the Bank Act would enable a bank to make advances upon the security of that grain. I do not see how one can differentiate between general grain and grain grown from seed purchased by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is correct in stating that once the crop is reaped and the grain harvested, if an agreement had been taken for a lien, it would probably be given effect to by the courts; but the section of the existing legislation to which I have referred does not cover the case of growing crops. As my hon. friend knows, growing crops are in a sense real estate and not personal property. We propose to give a lien analogous to the lien

which is given under legislation of certain of the provinces, in the West solely, so far as I am advised, by which legislation a lien may be given for advances made for the purchase of seed grain, upon the growing crop as well as upon its product when harvested and threshed.
Does the minister know whether the banks are prepared to avail themselves of this proposal if it is adopted?

Do not worry about
that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The banks must exercise
their discretion in regard to all applications for loans. It is not open to a government to enact compulsory legislation unless the further step is taken of supplying the financial institutions with money. The banks have to loan out money which is placed on deposits with them by the public throughout the country. It is for them to exercise their discretion as to whether or not in particular cases they will or will not extend credit. Our object in introducing this legislation is to enable a bank to take a lien, the idea being that, being able to take this additional security, it would be more willing to lend in a case in which there might be some doubt as to whether the loan was a good one or not. I believe that this legislation will facilitate the extension of credit to the farmers for the purpose of purchasing seed grain.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I presume
that this legislation is introduced in response to many requests which have come to my ihon. friend chiefly from western farming communities. I am under the impression that this is not the first time that similar legislation has been requested. There have been many efforts on the part of farming communities to (have the Bank Act amended in the way in which it is proposed to amend it temporarily. The question is not free from doubt as to whether or not such a departure from well-known banking principles will work satisfactorily. At all events, this legislation will serve as an experiment. I never could see why it could not be done. There are, of course, some conflicting principles. For instance, a moment ago my hon. friend said very properly that a standing crop is part of the realty. Under the present law of the province of Quebec, the crop would go to the purchaser of the soil. It is easy, however, by legislation to give a bank the necessary power to collect its lien. From
time to time the banking law has been amended to advance credit further so as to enable men to get accommodation from the banks. This is another step in that direction. It is an experiment, and I hope and believe it will woik out satisfactorily.

With one exception, I am quite in favour of the resolution as presented by the Minister of Finance. He brings it into effect only until the 1st of August, 1915. A provision of this character is of such value to the farming communities of western Canada in particular, that it should become a part of the Bank Act of Canada and should remain in force along with the other provisions of that Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my right hon. friend has put the matter very fairly in saying that such legislation has not in the past at least, been regarded as being free from doubt, and that this amendment is in the nature of an experiment. From the experiment which we shall make with this, we shall be in a better position to judge as to the advisability of adopting the suggestion put forward by my hon. friend. In the past, either this question specifically-or questions analogous to it-as to the security which may be taken by banks from their customers, has been very much discussed in the House and in the Banking and Commerce Committee. In the past one consideration as against legislation of this kind has had great weight with the House; that is, that the banker's lien is a secret lien, and one reason why Parliament has not been willing to permit banks to lend upon chattel security or to extend the list of securities upon which banks may lend money, has been that other creditors, who would not be aware of the existence of the lien, might be prejudiced, and that parties who had themselves taken a lien might find themselves cut out by a secret lien taken previously to their encumbrance, without notice on their part. Therefore the question is not entirely free from difficulty; but for the present year, and having regard to the exceptional situation which prevails, we think we may well enact this legislation, which, by the way, we intend shall date back to March 15, 1915. I notified the banks on the introduction of this resolution in order that any steps that they might take, immediately between March 15 and the date of the passage of this Bill, would be authorized and legalized by this legislation.
Mr. BUCHANAN1: I agree somewhat with the remarks of the hon. member for Strath-

cona (Mr. Douglas) in this respect. This is not compulsory upon the banks, but it gives them the right to do this, if they want to do so. If it were extended and made a feature of the Bank Act, it would rest with the banks as to whether they would make the ^advances or not. I think there is something to be said in favour of making it a permanent feature of the Act.
I would like to point out to the minister something which has relation to the condition in my own district, and which applied not only to seed grain, hut to feed for live stock. I think that in the recent amendments to the Bank Act provision was made whereby banks may lend money on the security of live stock. In my district great difficulty is experienced in securing feed for live ^tock. The Government is providing feed for work horses and some other farm animals, but I have received a great many complaints to the effect that the farmers are not in a position to borrow money from the banks to secure feed which will carry them through till harvest time. The owner of a large number of cattle or hogs or sheep who cannot get assistance from the Government is in the position that he cannot get assistance from the banks. He cannot get feed on credit, and he is forced to dispose of his live stock at a great sacrifice. I think that the banks should go out of their way to assist any farmers who have difficulties in that respect and of whose credit they are satisfied. I am led to believe, however, that the banks, without considering the credit of the farmer or the stock raiser, simply take the view that they will not lend money-and they are not lending it. Consequently, mixed farming in my section of the country is suffering severely by reason of the action of the banks in this respect. My criticism does not apply to all banks, because I know that some of the banks are treating the farmers fairly liberally in this respect. A great many of them, however, are not, and the result is that the farmers are losing their live stock. Although the banks may not avail themselves of any provision which may be made to obviate this difficulty, I would be glad if the Minister of Finance would urge upon them the desirability of their being more liberal in their treatment of the farmers, thus enabling the farmers to retain their live stock which they have purchased in recent years and which during the last season many of them have been forced to sacrifice on account of lack of feed. I received a communica-

tion this morning stating that the policy of the department was largely confined to providing feed for work horses in order that the crop should be put in this spring. I am told that the supplying of feed does not apply to milch cows; it is needless to say that it would be a serious matter for the farmers to have to sacrifice their milch cows at this time. Conditions are so critical that the farmer may lose many of their animals by being obliged to dispose of them at very small prices.

Any provision which
would enable the farmers to obtain credit certainly ought to commend itself to this committee. But I think in considering this measure one ought to bear in mind that the farmer would benefit by being enabled to get credit from storekeepers and from the people with whom he is accustomed to deal and from whom he is in the habit of getting his supplies. That brings up the consideration as to whether they or these bankers' liens should be secret. I do not believe that a banker's lien upon lumber or upon any other article ought to be a secret lien. If the banker takes a lien upon grain and upon the products of grain, I do not see why that lien should not be filed in the local registry office, so that everybody who chooses to make inquiry would be able to find out just what liens exist against a man who may be getting credit from the storekeeper or from any other person. By extending the banker's lien and still providing that it shall be secret, you hamper the farmers in getting credit from the persons with whom they have business transactions and the dealers from whom they may desire to purchase. Can my hon. friend suggest any reason why a banker's lien should be secret? If a man borrows from a private individual and gives a bill of sale, that bill of sale must be filed in the registry office. If he buys machinery on a vendor's lien or a lien note, that lien note must be filed in the registry office. That is the law; why should the banks be singled out for exceptional legislation and be allowed to make secret agreements? When the debtor finds himself unable to meet all his obligations, the banks may get in first and sweep away everything which the man has, leaving the other creditors absolutely without remedy or relief.
Mr. WHITE; My hon. friend has put forth very cogently the reasons which have usually been given in the House, in connection with the decennial revision of the

Bank Act, why the bankers' lien under section 88 of the existing legislation, should not be extended. The matter to which he refers was given very careful consideration by the Banking and Commerce Committee at the last revision, and was also discussed to some extent in the House. It was shown to the satisfaction of the committee that on account of the vast number of transactions, running up to a great number every day, which take place in this connection, it is inexpedient that the liens taken upon merchandise generally and lumber, to which my hon. friend particularly referred, should be registered. It was also shown to the satisfaction, I think, of the committee, that no disadvantage resulted to the community as a whole by reason of the existing legislation. Both the committee and the House were unwilling, however, to extend the principle of secret lien so as to enable the banks to take, let us say, chattel mortgages-mortgages upon all kind's of chattel property.
My hon. friend has said that he thinks it advisable that these liens should be registered, and there is much to be said for that view. But he will recognize that if a provision were made for registration, machinery would have to be created whereby the liens could be registered. The one great difficulty in the way at present is that in the province of Quebec such a thing as a chattel mortgage is not known; it is prohibited by law. There is in that province no provincial organization such as exists in the province of Ontario, let us say-and, I believe, in almost all the other provinces- whereby a mortgage, as we call it in Ontario, of that character, can be conveniently registered upon the payment of a small fee. It would be necessary, therefore, in connection with this measure which I am now introducing, if we decided that these liens should be registered, to create machinery in the province of Quebec for that purpose. A proposal of this kind would have to receive very careful and somewhat prolonged consideration. My hon. friend is not in disagreement with myself as to this. He evidently has in his mind that the farming community may be prejudiced in obtaining credit from storekeepers and others by reason of the possible existence of a lien in favour of the banks. There is also this view: that storekeepers and other creditors might be prejudiced by the existence of a secret lien of which they had no knowledge. That is the reason why Parliament in the past has not been willing to agree to the extension of the secret lien.
The seed grain situation this year is exceptional, because there appears without doubt to be a serious shortage of seed grain, especially in the West. The Government is doing what it can. I think we appropriated some $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 for the purpose of making advances to the farmers of the West in order to enable them to procure seed grain, which action is necessarily limited to those areas of the country which have been drouth-stricken because, speaking generally, when you deal with those who have patented their lands, as opposed to those who have not yet secured patents, who are the wards of the Government in a sense, any action of this character should be provincial rather than Dominion. If the Dominion assumed the task of financing any class of the community its action would have to be Dominion wide, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and I think it is common ground to both this Government and the Government which preceded it, as is shown clearly by the correspondence of 1908 with relation to seed grain advances, that once land is patented, prima facie, the duty of assisting those who had the patented lands devolves upon the provincial government. However, this has been an exceptional year, as was 1908; and the Government, as I have stated, decided to make very large advances to assist those in the drouth-stricken district to purchase seed grain. In order to carry out the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) to provide for the registration of these liens, much more consideration would be required than we are able to give to it this year or than the House would be able to give to it; and as the measure is temporary and as my right hon. friend has said in the nature of an experiment, and as it may be demonstrated by experience that this legislation may safely be made permanent, I think the Government are quite justified in introducing this measure to meet the exceptional situation which prevails.

The minister stated that this suggestion as to the registration of the liens had passed Parliament and the committee of Parliament when the Banking Act was up for discussion, to the satisfaction of Parliament and the committee. It probably did pass to the satisfaction of the majority of the House and the majority of the committee, but not with the unanimous sanction of Parliament or the committee, because it was pretty seriously discussed then and is a serious problem as was stated by the hon. member for St. John. The min-

ister says that no machinery exists or could be made to exist at the present time. It appears to me it would be the easiest thing in the world to devise machinery for the registration of these liens, that they could be registered with the clerk of the county court in each county and have a fee of 10 cents paid to the registrar or clerk of the court. Then every one would have notice that the bank did not have a lien. I for one think that the bank has altogether too much advantage over ordinary creditors throughout the country. They have the best of it all the way through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The banks have not asked for this legislation.
Certainly not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not introducing it at the instance of the banks, but at the instance of those who think it would facilitate the extension of credit in the West.

Quite so, but my hon. friend is failing to put in a clause providing for the registration of the lien at the instance of the bank. The banks do not want the lien registered, hut it should be registered.
Resolution reported, read the first and the second time and agreed to.
Hon. W. T. WHITE thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 78, to amend the Bank Act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called:
A few days ago I asked whether any Order in Council had been made providing for the appointment of a Committee of Council to deal with militia or war expenditures.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman alluding to orders from the British and foreign Governments or to expenditures by the Canadian Government?
Either or both, whichever the right hon. gentleman would give me information about.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There has been a sub-Committee of Council, not appointed in any formal way, in each case. They bring in their reports to Council, and anything that is done is the work of Council as a

whole, after the committee make their report, which is a very common mode of procedure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A committee composed of whom?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I really could not say from memory. It is quite a large committee. I will get that information.
The right hon. gentleman promised to give me the information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am bringing it down now. My hon. friend asked whether or not an Order in Council had been passed. I made inquiry and found that there was no Order in Council; but if it is desired that information should be given as to who were the members of the Committee of Council, I will get that; in fact, I have already given directions. It has not at all times been composed of the same ministers, as different members of Council have been added to it from time to time.
Was a separate committee appointed for the purpose of dealing with expenses made by the Canadian Government in connection with the war?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not sure
whether that would be done by the same committee or not, but it is my recollection that the committee was composed in the same way. I can ascertain about that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I notice by an answer that was given yesterday that certain purchases were made in the absence of the Minister of Militia. I presume these expenditures were made upon the report of that committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That would not necessarily follow. In the absence of the Minister of Militia, the matter would be taken up by the acting minister.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to provide that any insurance company whose power to apply for a license under the provisions of the Insurance Act, 1910, will expire before the end of the next session of Parliament, may obtain an extension of such power until the end of the next session of Parliament, by filing a notice in prescribed form with the Superintendent of Insurance, and paying a fee of one hundred dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Insurance companies,
which, under section 78 of the Insurance Act of 1910, are subjected to forfeiture of their charters unless they obtain a license within a period of two years after the granting of the charter, will by this Act be allowed, under certain conditions, to obtain an extension of that time. It was considered that under the existing circumstances there would probably be, or at all events there might possibly be, a fairly large number of companies whose two-year term would expire between now and the next session of Parliament and who, under existing conditions, would find it impossible or at all events very difficult to initiate their business before the expiry of the time limit. In fact, a certain number of applications have already been made and private Bills passed. It was also thought desirable to avoid passing the considerable number of private Bills that might have been presented by reason of these conditions, and we are in consequence making this extension general, subject to the condition that the companies must advance reasons why the time should be extended, and further that their time limit expires between now and the next session of Parliament. This Act will make it possible for companies filling that condition to obtain an extension of time, by filing a notice with the Superintendent of Insurance within two months after the passing of this Act.
This Bill, when passed, will not change the Acts under which these companies received their charters ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It will simply enable them to get an extension of that period of two years. Everything else will remain the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are doing something for them that in the ordinary course of events would have to be done by the passing of a private Bill, and the passing of a private Bill would cost more than $100. If it is proper that fees should be paid for private legislation, it seemed to us not improper that these companies should pay something-and I understand that $100 is less than what they would have to pay for a private Bill-for obtaining relief by this exceptional method.
It will not be necessary for them to obtain a private Bill P This fee covers the whole thing P

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Upon application, accompanied by this fee, the extension will be granted until the expiry of the next session of Parliament.
Then they would have to get a private Bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If they wanted a
further extension, but it may be doubted whether Parliament would grant a further extension to those companies that did not initiate their business before the end of the next session of Parliament. We are saving them from the difficulty that might be incurred between now and the next session of Parliament.
How many companies would this apply to ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not in a position to know how many companies will, between now and the next session of Parliament, have reached their time limit of two years from the date of their charter; but the Act will make it possible for all those companies to obtain an extension, provided they make application within two months of the passing of this Bill.
What has been the practice in the past with regard to a new charter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know of an
instance where a measure precisely of this character has been considered necessary or desirable, but as I said at the outset we believed, and that belief has been justified by a certain number of communications which have been received, that at the present session of Parliament we should have numerous applications of this kind; and one of the reasons that moved us in introducing this Bill was to relieve Parliament at this session of the necessity of dealing with possibly a very large number of such applications. In addition to that, there was reason to believe, in fact we had reason to know from a number of communi-actions received, that the present condition might make it difficult for companies to initiate their business within the prescribed time, although those companies might ultimately be in a position to start up in their business. Our principal object in bringing in this Bill was to enable us to deal by one measure with what we had reason to believe, and what I still believe, would have been a large number of applications for extensions, which in the past Parliament has made no great difficu'ty about granting.

The effect of tins measure is very wide. If the argument of my hon. friend holds good, there is no reason why the Government should not at any session of Parliament introduce legislation extending any railway charter, for instance, that might expire between two sessions of Parliament. That would be handing over to the Government the functions of this Parliament. It is this Parliament which grants the charters and whose function it is to determine whether that charter shall be renewed. My hon. friend is introducing a rather serious principle when he asks Parliament to abrogate its functions entirely, and to give up the right of scrutiny which the people's representatives here have in regard to all questions affecting the status of companies applying for charters, such as, whether their operations are bona fide, and all the other matters which Parliament ought to determine. If, as the minister says, this legislation is without precedent, it is a very important transgression upon the right of Parliament to deal with these matters. It means the transference from Parliament to the Government of important functions which hitherto have been vested solely in Parliament. Perhaps I may be wrong in my apprehension as to the effect of the measure, but I would judge, from what the minister says, that I am correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Parliament is not being asked to part with its power, save to a very limited extent, indeed. If this particular action is not justified by the exceptional circumstances, then I do not know that it would be justified at all. Parliament has. in view of the existing circumstances, confided to the Government very much wider and more important powers than the power that is involved in this resolution. It is a purely transitory measure. In two months from the date that the Bill is sanctioned, it will be absolutely without effect. It is only to meet a passing condition, and I think the hon. gentleman is unduly apprehensive in anticipating any serious consequences to be attached to it as involving any renunciation of any principle or the abandonment by Parliament of any of its powers.

With all due deference to my hon. friend, I fail to appreciate the force of his argument. Because Parliament has conveyed to the Government certain exceptional rights which they are supposed to exercise, and has given them power to deal with conditions which are

exceptional and which arise on account of the war, I fail to see a justification of the proposition, that, having given certain powers to railway and other companies possessing federal charters, these powers to be exercised within a certain period of time, we are to abandon altogether our right to scrutinize the actions of these companies and relinquish that power to the Government. It is not any condition resulting from the war that gives rise to this legislation. Why should not all these people whose charters were about to expire this year have given notice of their intention to apply to this House for an extension of time, and why should Parliament not have been asked to deal with this question in one case as well as in the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have put forward the reasons that I have to give to justify this legislation. I have endeavoured to be as clear as I could, and I have nothing further to add to what I have already said. If my reasons do not carry conviction to the mind of my hon. friend, I can only express my regrets.
Do I understand that the minister declines, or is unable, to tell us why these companies should not have given notice in the regular way?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have endeavoured to give the reasons. I have given all the reasons I have. I think they are satisfactory reasons but the hon. gentleman thinks they are not satisfactory.

I did not hear my
hon. friend give any answer to the question I am asking him now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
1 do not know why
they could not have done it, and I do not suppose they could not have done it. It would have been possible to do it. That is so obvious that I would have thought the hon. member would have known it without my telling him, but what I was pointing out was that we had reason to believe, and we did believe, tnat, owing to present conditions, a large number of these applications were exceedingly probable. There was a general desire that the business of this session should, as far as possible, be confined to matters arising out of the present condition of war. It was also desired that the session should not be unduly prolonged in attending to matters of this kind. Under these circumstances it was thought a proper thing to ask Parliament to confide to the Government of the day this power to be exercised during this limited period of two months. These are all the

reasons I have to give. I cannot say why it was Impossible for these companies to give notice and come to this House. I do not suggest that it was, and therefore I have no reason to offer in sunnort of any suggestion that it was impossible. It is for the House to say whether the reasons I have advanced, as forming the ground upon which this legislation is before the House, are sufficient but they do not imply that it was impossible to give notice.

Then I understand
the minister to say that he bases this legislation, which means the abnegation by Parliament of its rights, on the conditions created by the war? If my hon. friend puts it on that ground it is entirely different from the other ground.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I suppose everybody
will determine for himself what are the causes of the existing conditions.
Resolution reported, read the first and the second time, and agreed to.
Mr. DOHERTY thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 79,
4 p.m. to authorize certain extensions of time to insurance companies.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
Royal Nortiiwest Mounted Police, $1,406,691.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['Yes, these are new sections.']

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is a very substantial increase in this amount, due to the increase in the force which has been authorized by Parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
How many
men are there in the force now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are the police continuing the patrol of the northern waters?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, the same as in previous years. The controller informs me that the men who have been added to the force within the past year are of very good type. They have been very apt in learning their training and discipline and they are very effective members of the force.
"Mr. A. K. MACLEAN:	Are these additions to be permanent, or are they due to the war?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We thought it desirable to add to the force, but in view of the situation the usual time of enlistment was reduced, and the men have been enlisted for one year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Have any new arrangements been made with the Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan with regard to the force?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, and no. There has been correspondence of a confidential character with the Governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta which I shall be very glad to submit to my right hon. friend. In Saskatchewan matters stand precisely where they were under the arrangement made some years ago; and so far as I can gather it is the proposal of the Government of that province to have their own provincial police force. The same communications which were made to the Government of Saskatchewan were made to the Government of Alberta, but there has been a more extended correspondence with the Government of the latter province, the result of which is that I am confident we shall come to a satisfactory arrangement with the province of Alberta for the continuance of the force. The terms which were recommended to me by the controller and by the commissioner had my approval, and just two days ago we had what I think may be regarded as the



final reply of the Government of Alberta. That reply is of such a character that 1 think an agreement will be reached. As to Saskatchewan, I do not think there is any prospect of such an arrangement. We have not had any suggestion that the Saskatchewan Government would be inclined to have the arrangement continued. So far as Alberta was concerned, it was largely a question of the length of time for which the Alberta Government would be prepared to enter into an arrangement. We could not very well go to certain necessary expenditure in that province except for a fairly reasonable term. We represented that condition to the Premier of Alberta, who received it in a very reasonable way <md apparently saw the force of it. The letter which I have just received froan him will, I think, result in an arrangement which will be satisfactory to both Governments.

report.

speechtext:
I really could
not tell my hon. friend. * I will obtain the information and let him know.

Marine and Fisheries-Ocean and River Service-maintenance and repairs to Dominion steamers and ice-breakers, $1,125,000,
How many dredges are working in the river St. Lawrence?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This vote is to make provision for the maintenance and operation of the Ship Channel Dredging Fleet, as well as general additions to the machinery and plant. In answer to my hon. friend, I may say that we have eight elevator dredges with tugs, at $45,000 each, or $360,000 altogether; two new self-propelling steel -elevator dredges with tugs; one hydraulic dredge with two tugs; two suction hopper dredges; two self-propelling hopper barges; two dipper dredges with tugs; three inspection and sweeping tugs; three stone lifters and floating shop, and one rock cutter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does this include the whole channel, above arid below Quebec ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: From Montreal to the sea.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There was an accident last year near Father Point. Was it due to the state of the river or to some fault on the part of the ship?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The state of the river had absolutely nothing to do with the accident.

Did the minister ever consider whether it would not be cheaper to have this work done by contract? I have always considered, and think now, that it would be far cheaper for the Government to have this work done by contract, providing the tenders were properly called for and properly let, and the contractors held up to their contracts, as they should be. I feel sure that would be a cheaper method than having the work done by the Government, because it is a well-known fact that the Government dredges do not do in a day more than (half the work that is done by contractors under their terms of contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That has not been our experience so far as the work on the ship channel is concerned. The work is being done under the same system as when I

became minister. The work is in charge of Superintendent V. W. Forneret, C.E.
I can give my hon. friend some figures as to the cost. The work is carried on by these dredges owned by the Government and supplies in the way of food, etc., are furnished by contracts entered into with different people. The repair work is done at the ship yard at Sorel. The figures as to cost with reference to the different dredges Which I shall mention, include repairs and everything else, with the exception of the charge for interest on capital outlay. First, taking the dredge Labelle, we find that the cost of removing stone and gravel was $1.21 a yard; dredge Laurier, working in clay, shale rock and hard pan, 26 cents; dredge Lady Minto, clay, 19 cents; Baldwin, 19 cents; Israel Tarte, shale rock, 32 -cents, and Galveston, 8 cents. The average cost of removing material in the way we are doing is considerably less than if the work were done by tender and contract as suggested by my hon. friend.

Does the department
keep -any account of the extra -cost based upon interest and depreciation of plant ? Is there no estimate made of that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think that we have any statement made up to date, but it is an easy thing to get at. We know what the plant has cost and, allowing interest on the cost, we h-ave found it considerably less than if we were to ask for tenders. Apart from that there is the -advantage of having, the work done under one uniform system and with one -superintendent having control of -the whole work. The work is very important and very good results lare being obtained from it. I am disposed to think that it is a better system than if we asked for tenders for different parts of the work.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Can my hon. friend give us any information as to the actual condition of the channel between Montreal and Quebec ? What is the average depth and width ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The work between Montreal and Quebec is progressing very satisfactorily. I-n all places there is a depth of 30 feet, and work is now going on to extend the depth to 35 feet. The -channel is being widened and straightened by degrees. The aim is to widen it to 500 feet. We started at 200 feet, it has been widened to 300 feet, and we propose to extend it to a uniform width of 500 feet with a uniform depth of 35 feet, and to make the channel
straighter. This is necessary on 'account of the larger ships that are now coming up to Montreal. The work is proceeding satisfactorily. In some places the channel is down to a depth of 30 feet, although it will take some time before the work is entirely completed. There was an inquiry made in reg-ard t-o the lowering
5 p.m. of the water in consequence of this deepening of the channel, and a commission was appointed a year or two ago composed of Dr. Haskell, dean of the engineering faculty of Cornell university, Mr. Stewart, superintendent of the ship -channel, and Mr. Stewart, chief of the hydrographic survey. These gentlemen have made their report, which report was laid on the table of the House a day or two ago. There was an apprehension that it would be necessary to put in reclamation works that would cost 'an enormous sum of money, but that has been dissipated entirely by the report. The report says that there has been a lowering in the harbour of Montreal of 2 feet 7 inches, that about two -or three inches is due to the diversion of water through the Chicago drainage canal from lake Michigan and that the balance is due to the work on the St. Lawrence channel and particularly due to the removal of obstructions at St-. Mary's rapids a little below Montreal. The effect of the removal of the obstructions has; been to allow the water to run out with more-freedom and cause a lowering of something over two feet in the water in the harbour of Montreal. Below that point the lowering has not been nearly so great. The report, shows how, in carrying on the ordinary-work for the improvement of the channel each year, dams can be constructed at a point below Montreal, where the river runs into lake St. Peter, by placing there the spoil that is taken from the river. In this way the level of the water can be raised and it is estimated that the total cost of this work will not exceed $400,000. Perhaps it will be a little over $400,000. The work can be done as the ordinary work of deepening the channel proceeds. I think the report is calculated to remove apprehensions from the minds of those who thought that the work going on in the St. Lawrence river was going to do a great deal of injury in the way of making very low water in the harbour of Montreal and above that point. The work is proceeding under the same system from year to year.
We had hoped to have the entire northern channel below the city of Quebec, which will be a much safer channel for navigation

after it is improved than the one on the south side of the river, finished by April. Last year we entered into a contract with the Canadian Vickers Limited of Montreal for the construction of a most modern dredge that would have facilitated that work. The work on the construction of the dredge was commenced, but unfortunately for reasons connected with the war, the work has had to be put to one side for the preseent. The delivery of the dredge will be delayed for probably a year, but that is something that is not under the control of the department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Have you commenced the work of dredging the northern channel?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, we are working on it now and we have made considerable progress but with the dredges we have my recollection is that it will take perhaps six or seven years to complete the work. With this modern dredge about which I have spoken we could have had the work completed in less than half that time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In regard to the channel between Montreal and Quebec, I understand that the report of the commission to which my hon. friend has referred suggests that the refuse which is taken from the river should be placed between the islands at the entrance to lake St. Peter?
Mr*. HAZEN: That is it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would that have any effect upon the flooding of that part of the country which is very low?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When the work is finished it will have no effect on the flooding.
If you put a dam in the river to raise the level of the water at Montreal, you will have to build a dyke.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is no need for a
dyke.
They are what are called wing dams.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Something of that sort.

The minister should
ascertain from his engineers just what work is necessary to deepen the river between Montreal and Quebec, and then advertise for tenders and let the work by contract. In tnat way he would get the work done more expeditiously and more satisfactorily. The work has been dragging on for twelve or fifteen years-I do not know that this

Government is any more to blame than the former Government-and it ought to have been finished long ago. This is an important work to the shipping interests and the Government have a lot of dredges of their own, working eight hours a day ostensibly, but really not working more than six and not -working very rapidly even at that, so that you are getting practically nothing done. This work will drag out till doomsday.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is not fair to say we
are getting nothing done. Until compar-ratively few years ago the channel between Montreal and Quebec was only fourteen feet deep. Finally we got an average of thirty feet, and it is now found that thirty feet is not sufficient for the large steamers plying to Montreal. The channel has to be deepened to thirty-five feet and it has also been found necessary to widen and straighten it so as to make navigation safer. I believe the work is proceeding as satisfactorily as possible. It may be that even when we get the channel thirty-five feet deep and 500 feet wide, in the future it will require further deepening and widening to accommodate larger steamers. So far as I am capable of judging, I think the work has been carried on well, and there is a uniformity about it which would not be possible if we were to award it to different contractors year after year. We have a competent man at the head, in Mr. Forneret, who understands the conditions and is there year after year. I believe we get a more satisfactory return for the money we spend than we could in any other way.

My experience is that the
Government dredges we have had in the harbour of Yarmouth have not done the work as satisfactorily or as expeditiously as the work could be done under tender and contract. The Government dredges do not work the number of hours that the private dredges do, and they do not seem to do the work so well. I must say that because I have had some experience. Taking it altogether, I believe that the Government could let the work by contract and save money.
Do you find that this channel fills up and that the work has to be done year after year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. Every year when navigation opens we sweep the channel, because it was found once or twice that boulders

lodged in the channel during the winter. We have no trouble from the ordinary filling in with silt.
What does this dredging cost per cubic yard?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have the returns here dredge by dredge, and it costs from five cents per cubic yard up to seventy cents per cubic yard. It depends upon the nature of the material. In places where there is a heavy rise and fall of tide, or where dredges cannot work steadily because of rough weather, the cost would be greater than in the St. Lawrence, where there is not that difficulty to contend with. Then there are certain modern dredges that will do more work in the same time than dredges of an earlier date. The average cost for 1914 was 14-75 cents per cubic yard, but that does not include a charge for interest on the cost of the machinery.
Neither uepreeiation nor interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, but it includes the cost of all repairs. The dredges are kept in the very best state of repair.
These figures would hardly be a fair criterion to show the cost of the dredging to the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Every winter these dredges axe overhauled at Sorel and put in the best possible condition, and the cost of these repairs is included in the average I have given.

Some of these dredges must cost quite a lot of money, and to get a fair estimate of what the ultimate cost of the dredging is, the interest should be charged.
Mr. RAZ.EN: That is quite true.
Marine and Fisheries-to provide for construction and completion of dredging plant for river St. Lawrence from Montreal to Father Point, $871,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is a portion of this
that we shall not be called upon to pay this year, because the woi-k will not be completed upon the self-propelling elevator dredge which was to have been delivered to us by the close of this season. I do not believe we shall get delivery of it until the close of 1916.
How much has been expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The amount put in for the dredge is $500,000, of which I do not believe that more than 50 per cent will bo expended.
About $250,000 will not be required. Why not reduce the item by that amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The war may end very
suddenly, and there is always a chance that more progress may be made than we expect at the present time. This is the amount that was voted by Parliament last year for the work. We thought it advisable to leave it in for that reason.

The Minister of Finance has made items like this an excuse for the extra taxes. I believe there are millions of dollars just like this $250,000 which will not be required. My hon. friend will see how much better it would be if this item -were left out. I do not single this out especially, but it is on a par with many other items.
The whole amount might very well be omitted.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The whole amount cannot be omitted. We expended in 1913-14, $695,613.
Has the dredge been started yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is under way.
Is the work suspended now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, for reasons which I cannot explain. The House will understand.
New ice-breaker for river St. Lawrence, $500,000.
is that a revote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. A great deal of progress has been made on this vessel. But for the war it would have been delivered to us at the opening of the season. It is expected by the people in charge of the work that the vessel will be ready for us, if not at the close of this season, then by the opening of next season. The vessel is being built by Canadian Vickers, Ltd., of Alontreal, that firm being the lowest tenderer.
Has the Earl Grey been formally disposed of to the Russian Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Has the minister arranged to get a new ice-breaker in place of the Earl Grey?

speakerposition: subtopic
Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We are getting this new icebreaker built, which will be of much greater power, and which will be an icebreaker alone. It will not be used for any other purpose. It was found by the department to have an ice-breaker that does icebreaking at certain seasons and other work during other portions of the year, is not good business, as the vessel will consume a tremendous amount of coal to have the necessary power. With the putting on of the car ferry across the Northumberland strait from Cape Tormentine on the mainland to Cape Traverse on the island, and the railway travel going by that means, there would not be much use for the Ear] Grey on the route on which it was in the past. We think we shall not require to order another ice-breaker, with the two others that we have on the island route during the winter, and that we shall be able to get on tery well until this new icebreaker is completed.
lighthouse and coast service-agencies, rents and contingencies, $150,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the increase of $15,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is due to the annual increases in the salaries of agents and clerks in the various agencies, authorized by the schedule established in April, 1911. While those clerks are not in the inside service, there was adopted a schedule of salaries for the different positions, so that they could get certain annual increases just as do the clerks in the inside service. There were additions to the staffs of some of the agencies owing to increased work and extended premises. This is a summary of the proposed expenditure: Nova Scotia, including subagencies at Sydney and Pictou, $30,800; New Brunswick, $13,150; Prince Edward. Island, $8,850; Quebec, $36,450; Montreal, $13,300; Ontario, $3,200; Parry Sound, $5,100; Kenora subagency, $700; Fort William, $1,800; Victoria, including Prince Rupert, $22,800; contingencies, etc., $13,850; total, $150,000. The Fort William agency is a new one. We used to make arrangements in different ways for the work there, but that plan cost practically as much and was not as satisfactory as having an agency of our own. Therefore, we established an agency there. We have also had some additions in connection with the agency at Prince Rupert in consequence of the development of that portion of the Pacific coast.

Has the minister decided finally and unalterably to construct the new

signal service at Point Abine, about which he has had a considerable amount of correspondence, so as to wind up that little ball of yarn at once?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have had considerable
communication with different gentlemen on this subject. Steamers coming from Buffalo pass by that point, and the Government of the United States asked us to construct a fog alarm there, which we agreed to do. Opposition to its construction was offered by a number of summer residents in the locality, who had the impression that they would be disturbed by the sound of the fog alarm. During the season when the summer residents are there, however, there is very little fog on the lakes, and they would suffer very little inconvenience in that respect. Having lived in St. John much of my life, I have become rather fond of the sound of the fog horn. I think that the inconvenience which the summer residents anticipate is more fancied than real, and that after the fog alarm is in operation a month or two they will not notice it at all. Their interests ought to be considered, however, and we are trying to make arrangements with the United States Government whereby this fog alarm will be used only in cases of necessity during the summer months.
Subject to that arrangement, the fog alarm will be established?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, the work will be proceeded with.

Is the agency at
Pictou a subagency of Halifax, or of Charlottetown?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Halifax.
Salaries and allowances to lightkeepers, $450,000.
Does this amount cover the allowances made to lightkeepers all over Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. This vote is for the
purpose of providing salaries for superintendents of lights, lightkeepers and crews of lightships. For the fiscal year 1912-13 the expenditure was $415,294.47; for 1913-14, $420,616.13. We are asking for the same appropriation for this year.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to inquire from the hon. the Minister of Marine why the lighthouse keeper at Pointe au Prere is not put on the

same footing as the other keepers stationed along the coast.
Since we have been in power, that is since September, 1911, the lighthouse keeper at Pointe au Prere is without telegraphic means of communication at his station, while at every other station along the St. Lawrence lighthouse keepers have remained m possession and retain the use of telegraph facilities.
On a previous occasion' I drew the attention of the hon. gentleman to that fact. 1 do not know whether he did not catch my meaning or else was adverse to granting my request, but at all events I am from year to year in receipt of complaints from that keeper, stating that he is debarred from the use of telegraphic facilities, and I realize that he has good reason to complain. Whenever he wishes to know whether there are vessels coming up or down the St. Lawrence he is under the necessity of walking a distance of four or five arpents to reach the place where the telegraph office is now located.
It. seems to me his station should not be on a different footing from that of other lighthouses, unless the intention is to discriminate, and I for one am inclined to consider it in that light, since all other lighthouse keepers have the use of telegraphic facilities.
At Matane, in the constituency I represent, there is a telegraph station in the village. I do not see why at Pointe au Prere, which is a much more important station than Matane and many others, the keeper should not have the benefit of telegraph facilities. Under present arrangements, he is left completely in the dark as regards the movements of vessels up and down the St. Lawrence. To secure information in that respect he must go over a distance of four or five arpents, and apply to a man who is not always of a disposition to facilitate matters for him. I say that such a state of things is intolerable and should not be allowed to exist whether in Rimouski or any other constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend sees now the mistake he made in depriving the country of the services of Mr. McWilliams. He should have been retained in the service.
Does the Government pay any amount for the use of the telegraph ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We are paying nothing to Mr. McWilliams in connection with the telegraph service, but I think he is the signal officer there. It is most desirable and in the public interest that the signal service officer should be the man who is the telegraph operator at the place in question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would suggest that everybody would be pleased, the hon. member for Rimouski included, if Mr. McWilliams was re-instated in the office from which he was dismissed.

My hon. friend should not be too hard upon the Minister of Fisheries for keeping friends of hon. gentlemen opposite in positions. Hon. gentlemen opposite should not. criticise him for that; he has always shown consideration for their friends.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Exactly, and the man who is dismissed from the service suffers accordingly.
Maintenance and repairs to lighthouses, $750,000.
Mr.'A. K. MACLEAN: Is that the amount usually expended in o-ne year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Last year we expended of this amount $699,785. LTp to the 31st of December last, for the present fiscal year, we expended $566,444. Up to the end of February we spent $645,361.22. This money is used to maintain aids to navigation, for supplies, fuel, illuminants, cleaning materials, delivering supplies and repairs to aids to navigation. A considerable number of lighthouses have been established during the present fiscal year and doubtless there will be further additions during this year. The humane establishments at Sable island and St. Paul's island will be paid out of this vote. Formerly this was paid out of the life-saving vote.

What is the
amount of repair expenditures, roughly?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: By provinces; in Nova Scotia, $166,000; in Prince Edward Island, $22,000; in New Brunswick, $96,000; in Quebec, $183,000; in Montreal, $24,000; in Ontario, $97,000; in British Columbia, $83,000; and on general account, $25,898.
Did the minister receive any request to establish telephone communication between Pictou island in Northumberland strait and the mainland?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, my recollection is that we received a communication asking us, in connection with the life-saving station there, to establish either a telephone or telegraph line to the mainland. We are making inquiries as to the cost and necessity of that work. That would come under the life-saving stations vote.

I do not know whether the cable already laid between Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island could be utilized in connection with the work I have suggested. It passes in the immediate vicinity of Pictou island and on account of its having been laid the people on the island felt that it might be used to afford them some communication with the mainland. I hope the minister will be able to give favourable consideration to the suggestion. Many islands on the coast have telegraphic communication with the mainland through tire Department of Public Works. There is a telegraph cable from Cape Tormentine to Traverse and a telephone cable was laid by the steamers of the Department of Public Works last year from Caribou on the mainland, passing in the immediate vicinity of Pictou island.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know whether it is feasible to have a branch cable connecting with this one across the straits. The cable was not laid by the Marine Department; I understand it was laid by the Nova Scotia Telephone Company and some of the Government steamers rendered assistance in laying it. Possibly we could make arrangements with the Nova Scotia Telephone Company to connect a cable from Pictou island with this one, but our justification for doing so would be that it would be of advantage to the life-saving station. That would be the only ground on which we could do it.

It would be justifiable on that ground because the life-saving station is about 9 mile' from any port
TMr. Hazen.l
where the assistance of a steamer could be secured. Such a connection as has been suggested would enable people living on the island to communicate with the mainland in any case of urgency.
Construction of lighthouses and aids to navigation, including apparatus, submarine signals, and providing suitable boats for carrying on construction work, $750,000.
Will the minister indicate what new lighthouses he proposes to build in Nova Scotia during the present year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I cannot indicate the amount we are going to spend on lighthouses in Nova Scotia. My hon. friend knows the system that prevails, that as applications are made they are submitted to the consideration of the Lighthouse Board who pronounce upon	their necessity. The
Lighthouse Board meets from time to time	and	receives applications.
The principal works to he carried out next season are as follows: Establishment of a new depot at Dartmouth, 845,000. We were conducting the naval depot at Halifax on the property that belonged to the Imperial Government, but we have practically been driven out of there since t'he war started; so we have removed the depot to Dartmouth, to the property purchased by the late Government six or seven years ago.

The Troop
property?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Was that sold?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We purchased the whole property from Mr. Troop. That portion with the dwelling-house on it has been sold, and we have been using the other portion with the buildings on it; and to properly equip these will take $45,000. Then certain protection work has to be done at Flat Point, at the mouth of Sydney Harbour. A new light is required at Negro Island, and a new tower at Peggy Point.
Where is Peggy Point?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Somewhere to the west of Halifax.
Is there not already a light at Negro Island?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, but the Lighthouse Board recommends that a new light be put up there. A new light is required for Caribou Island; range lights for Sheet Harbour; a fog alarm for Digby Gut; new apparatus for Cheticamp and Cape St.

Mary; rebuilding burned lighthouse at St. Paul Island; and a new light and fog-alarm apparatus at Scutari. That is as much as I can tell my hon. friend about the work to be done in Nova Scotia.
All these works have been recommended by the Lighthouse Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Does the minister propose to have this work done by tender and contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In nearly all cases our
work is done by tender and contract. But in some cases where the tenders are very high, the Chief Engineer recommends that the Government do the work by day labour, under an inspector appointed by the Engineering Branch of the Marine Department With that exception, contracts are let whenever the amount is over a few thousand dollars.
It is not customary to advertise for tenders in the newspapers. I think the practice is to send notices out in different post offices and to well-known contractors?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is the case with the
smaller jobs; the larger ones are advertised generally.

I think that was the practice followed by the late Government. Do the officials of the department send notices of these tenders to the men whose names were on file in the department as light-house builders, before the change of Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The deputy says we have
no such list. In the case of the. smaller light-houses the notices are put up in the post offices. In the case of larger works, they are generally advertised in the district where they are to be erected.

I had the impression that
the department sent out notices of these tenders to men who were known to the department as responsible contractors.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The deputy says he thinks not. He says that shortly after the notices are published in the post offices we receive inquiries for specifications from people who are always on the look-out for that kind of work.

The reason I bring the matter up is because from day to day I am requested by contractors in my own county
to see that their manes are filed with the Department of Marine hnd Fisheries, as persons who would be likely to tender for such contracts; but if that is not the practice nothing would be gained by forwarding the names to the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The deputy tells me there is no such list in the department.

I presume that the
depot at St. John will be paid for out of this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

How is work on the St. John wharf progressing? I have seen it stated, I am not sure whether it was in the newspapers, but certainly in communications that I have received, that some trouble had arisen by reason of the settlement of the concrete.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My attention was called to the newspaper paragraph to which my hon. friend alludes. I at once saw the chief engineer of the department, and the assistant engineer, Mr. Fraser. Mr. Fraser has had a great deal to do with the construction of this wharf, and he had just returned from St. John. He told me that there was nothing at all serious the matter, or which would add in any appreciable way to the expense. He said that the wharf when completed would be capital in every respect. There has been some little settlement, I understand, at one part of the wharf, but Mr. Fraser says it can be remedied without any trouble. Both he and Colonel Anderson assured me that I need have no apprehensions as to its safety or security.
What was the contract price?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: What did the site cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Somewhere about $60,000.
What is to be erected at Digby Gut?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A fog alarm.
A new one?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
In addition to the one that is there now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, inside.
How much will it cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Is it necessary to have two fog alarms there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The application came from the steamboat people who are running boats across the bay, and the Lighthouse Board recommended it.
I do not see the necessity for another fog alarm there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They say that inside the
Gut you cannot hear the fog alarm at all.
When you are inside, you don't need to hear it. I have crossed the bay a great many times and have always been able to hear the fog alarm from quite a distance.
Does the minister propose to locate the depot at Dartmouth permanently, or to use Halifax later?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is very difficult to get a convenient site along the water-front in Halifax at a reasonable price. Our idea is that we should use the site purcljased by the previous Government, I think, with the idea of a marine depot in view. There was a little difficulty at Halifax, on account of the men crossing and recrossing the water, but we can overcome that by a boat. We think on the whole it would be better at Dartmouth.
What proceeding is followed after an application has been received for the construction of a lighthouse?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Lighthouse Board consists of the deputy minister, the chief engineer of the Marine and Fisheries Department, the inspector of lights of the Marine and Fisheries Department, the chairman of the Dominion Marine Association, and the chairman or some man appointed by the Shipping Federation of Canada.
In many cases these gentlemen are familiar with the localities where these aids to navigation are or should be placed. The chief engineer of the department, who has been there for over forty yeaTS, is familiar with every lighthouse in Canada. I believe that he could sit down, and, starting at a point on the coast, point to the place where each lighthouse is located. Mr. McPhail is also familiar with this matter. For many years Mr. Andrew Allan has been a member of the board as the representative of the Shipping Federation of Canada. These gentlemen have a good deal of knowledge within themselves. If they have not the knowledge within themselves they may get it by an examination of the chart, or they
LMr. Hasten.]
may get it from the reports of the inspector of lights, or from the agents of the Marine Department, while in some eases they utilize officials in obtaining information in regard to lights.
Who succeeded Mr. Allan on the board ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is still on the board.

Since the appropriation was voted the other night for schools of navigation, I have received a letter from the teacher of the school of navigation at Yarmouth, in which he says that the opening of the free schools at Halifax and St. John has taken away about all his pupils. The school at Yarmouth is one of the oldest schools of navigation in Nova Scotia. It has turned out as many masters and mates as 'any other school in the maritime provinces. It would be quite a hardship if Yarmouth were deprived of this school altogether, as it serves the community from Lunenburg to Annapolis. The pupils are so few that it will be necessary to close the school altogether. On behalf of the western part of the province I would like to ask the minister to take the matter into his serious consideration and not allow this old, representative school to be displaced by these schools in Halifax and St. John. I am convinced that this teacher, who has done such good work, would be prepared to perhaps take a little less salary than the salaries paid at the schools in Halifax and St. John. I would ask the minister to take it into his consideration and see whether it would be possible to have the school at Yarmouth retained.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think there is a great deal in what my hon. friend says. I would be very sorry indeed to see Yarmouth left without a school of navigation. It is an important point from the marine standpoint. Up to -a few years ago students at St. John and Halifax who wanted to get the necessary education in navigation had to go to Yarmouth. The opening of these schools at St. John and Halifax has perhaps drawn them away to some extent from the Yarmouth school. I will give this matter my very sympaihic consideration.
I would like to ask the minister if he is aware that some boats struck rocks last season about two miles from the shore of the St. Lawrence opposite S;te. Felicite.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: AVhat are the names of the ships ?	.

I do not remember the names. One had to unload her cargo before she could get out, and she was badly damaged. The other one only touched something, but nobody could say what it was. I would like to know if these facts have come to the knowledge of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not recollect -any such circumstances at the present time, but I will endeavour to get the information for my ho-n. friend. I will ask the deputy to make a note of it.
