Bill No. 44, respecting certain patents of the Lohmann Company

Mr. Fripp-in Committee.
Has the minister looked into this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes, I was present when the Bill was discussed in the committee. This patent has been kept alive and the fees have been paid in full, but where they were in default was that the patentee died shortly before the time had elapsed for them to come under the license system.

This is the ugual Bill to revive a patent. They have not complied with the terms of the patent and they come here to ask special legislation to get a license to do certain things, and that without- manufacturing necessarily in Canada. Many times the question has been discussed in this House as to the wisdom of reviving these patents, and in every case, unless some Special cause has been shown, I have dissented to such legislation. What are the special circumstances here?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I have always taken
the position that where a patent has been allowed to expire, because the fees have not been paid, the patent should not be revived, and that course has been followed in several cases this session. In the present case the fees have been paid. Under the Patent Act, they can within six months after the patent has been issued, get a
license on making application, but in this case the patentee died a month or two before the expiry of that period, and this legislation is simply to put them in a position to apply for a license according to the Act.
What is the nature of this patent?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The Bill is in charge of Air. Fripp, and, as he is not present, if the hon. gentleman wishes, it can stand.

My attitude in regard to such legislation as this always has been to oppose giving the patentee rights, after the expiry of the time provided for in the patent, unless perchance the article is manufactured in Canada. If the article were manufactured in Canada, I would he disposed to give the patentee any privileges that were possible; but, as that is not the case, there ought to be the fullest explanation in each case, and the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) ought to give us that explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member. I am just as strongly opposed to the granting of these renewals as he is. I went into thi-s case very fully with the deputy, minister, -before I consented in the committee to support the renewal of this patent. I would prefer that a much fuller explanation be given to the committee, and therefore I am willing that the Bill should stand.

Last year I impressed on the Minister of Agriculture the desirability of having some amendments made to the Act, if it were desirable to have these privileges granted. If not, we ought to adhere to the Act, except in the most exceptional cases and only where it is m the interest of the country and not in the interest of the patentee that it should be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I drew the attention of the committee to the fact that applications for the renewal of patents had been increasing in number for many years. The committee unanimously came to the conclusion that we should very carefully investigate each care. It will be apparent from the results accomplished this session that the committee have done good work.
Progress reported.
Bill No. 55, to incorporate Vancouver Terminal Railway Company, and recom-

mending that the title be changed to an Act to incorporate Fraser Valley Terminal Railway Company-Mr. Stevens-in committee.
On section 1-name:
I would suggest that the Bill stand over until Monday, because the promoter is not here.

I do not think this Bill should stand over until Monday. It is a matter of great importance to the promoters to have this Bill pass through the Senate. I am prepared to give the committee any information desired with respect to it. It has been thoroughly thrashed out before the Railway Committee.

I was in the Railway Committee on the first occasion on which this Bill came up. It was fully discussed for an hour or an hour and a half, and by a substantial majority the committee killed the Bill. Later a motion was made in the House to refer the Bill back to the Railway Committee. I did not oppose that motion although I had very strong opinions adverse to the principles of the Bill. The motion was passed, and the Bill went back to the committee. On the same day and at the same hour at which the Railway Committee was sitting, I was engaged on another committee, and I had no opportunity of being in the Railway Committee when this Bill was under discussion; but I understand that many amendments were made of a far-reaching and substantial nature. Since then the Bill has not been reprinted, and it has been amended out of all recognition as compared with its original condition. I am glad of that, because the original Bill, in my opinion, was a highly improper one. As the committee should be properly informed as to the nature of the amendments, and as it cannot be properly informed unless the Bill is printed as amended, and as the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) in whose name the Bill stands is not here, I think the Bill should stand. Monday is a day which, if necessary, can be devoted entirely to private Bills, and there is plenty of time for the Bill to be considered in committee then. I am not taking the ground of opposing this Bill; but there were some very obnoxious clauses in it, and I had sound objections to the principles of certain of its clauses. I would like a proper opportunity to consider the amendments. I am not desirous of blocking the progress of the

Bill. There is ample time for it to go through.

The preamble of the Bill was killed the first time the Bill came up for discussion in the Railway Committee, owing to the stand taken by the hon. member in whose name the Bill stood. The Bill was referred back to the Railway Committee. That committee took it up the other day, and struck out the clause that was obnoxious to the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens.) That meant that this terminal company would not have any of the rights which it had in the original Bill, all reference to Vancouver having been cut out. In addition to that, the only other amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver was adopted by the committee, with the exception of one word which the hon. Minister of Railways agreed should be cut out also. The only reason why I should like this Bill to go through is that it has been thoroughly discussed for two days in the committee. After the amendments made by the hon. member for Vancouver had been accepted, the committee passed the Bill practically unanimously. I do not see any good reason why the Bill should stand over, because the session is getting very short and it has to go to the Senate, and the promoters are anxious to have the Bill go through. If the hon. member for Vancouver was foiled in any amendment that he wished to make before the committee, there would be some reason for having the Bill stand over. The amendments to the Bill are not very far reaching; some of the sections having been cut out, and the objectionable features of the last section of the Bill having been corrected by the committee to meet the wishes of the hon. member for Vancouver.
Perhaps the hon. member for Westminster (Mr. Taylor) will explain the Bill.

This Bill gives authority to a company, owning a large area of property on Lulu island, in the constituency that I represent, to make connection with the several railways, namely, the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern and the Northern Pacific principally, running into the Fraser valley. The essence of the Bill is the section giving permission to the company to run lines from its terminal at the extremity of Lulu island to all these railways. In committee, after the Bill was referred back, all reference to Vancouver city was struck out, because Vancouver had

126t
represented to the committee that the Bill as presented interfered with a certain agreement between that city and the Canadian Northern and Canadian Pacific railways. That being the case, no other objection on the part of the city of Vancouver or of any other interest remained. It is vital to the interest of an important part of my constituency that the promoters of this enter-prize be given the opportunity they desire to develop the dock and harbour works which they have in contemplation and which this Bill will enable them to connect with the railways. As to the alterations made in committee, nothing new was inserted in the Bill except a section at the end safeguarding the contract of the city of Vancouver, and a couple of standard clauses which were inserted at the instance of the chairman of the committee. The amendments made in committee consisted mainly of striking out what seemed to be unnecesarily liberal provisions. I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) that it is essential to the safety of this Bill that it should not be delayed at this late stage of the session, and I would suggest to the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) that his purpose would be served if he would discuss any objections as the different sections are reached in this committee.

I am not opposing this Bill, nor am I concerned in it except from the standpoint of the public interest. The amendments are difficult to understand; they appear to change the whole character and nature of the Bill. I am quite willing that the Bill should be proceeded with, if that is the desire of the committee, and if proper explanations can be given with regard to the proposed amendments.
I think the hon. member is mistaken as to the nature of the amendments. I will send him a copy of the Bill which, I think, will reassure him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This service collects and distributes information of the movements of vessels on the Great Lakes, in the river and gulf of St. Lawrence and on the Atlantic coast of Canada. ' It also reports ice and weather conditions. The service is also extensively used by the lighthouse and buoy service of the river St. Lawrence ship channel in connection with dredging. The expenditure for the fiscal year 1913-14 was $46,296 and the expenditure up to the 31st of December, 1914, during this fiscal year, was $39,271, so that the expenditure this year will apparently be about the same as last year. The stations are equipped to receive the reports by flag signals.
Where is the signal office at St. John?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the custom house There is also an official employed on Partridge island in connection with the Marconi station.
I was wondering whether this included the wireless station.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The only thing it includes in connection with wireless is $200 paid to a man on Partridge island. The operator at St. John is Mr. H. P. Butler, with offices in

the customs, house. He has been in the service a considerable number of years. He has an asistant, Mr. C. A. Cromwell.
What does the officer at Partridge island do?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The deputy tells me that
some arangement was made with the Marconi Company for one of their operators to do this work. That acounts for the $200.
Who is he employed by, the Government or the Marconi Company?

The Marconi Company,
under arrangement with the Government.
' Mr. PUGSLEY:	I have been requested
from St. John to get some information as to the three other gentlemen who are em-employed on Partridge island.
i Mr. HAZEN:	I think you will have to
ask the Militia Department about that. I presume my hon. friend refers to three gentlemen who are acting as censors, Mr. Masters, Mr. Crockett, and Mr. Shaw. They are paid by the Militia Department.

I have the best feeling in the world for these three gentlemen, more particularly Mr. Masters and Mr. Shaw, ' whom I am acquainted with, but there is a feeling of curiosity in St. John as to what the duties and salaries of these gentlemen are. Mr. Shaw is a lawyer and knows nothing about wireless telegraphy; no more does Mr. Masters.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These men are censors. All the telegrams passing through that station have to pass through their hands. If it would not be in the public interest to publish any of the despatches, I presume these gentlemen would submit the point to Major Hamilton here in Ottawa, who is the chief censor. All I know about these men is that I was asked by the Militia Department if I could recommend three suitable gentlemen, and I recommended the three men whose names I have mentioned, thinking they were suitable in every way.

Nobody would go to
Partridge island to send a wireless message. Messages would he caught 'by the wireless instrument there and forwarded on, so I do not see how these gentlemen, unless they are familiar with the wireless system, can be of any advantage-unless the messages are translated by the operator and submitted to them for inspection.
[Mr. Hazen.J

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I expect that is what happens.
Does my hon. friend not know what they receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They receive a certain sum per day; I am not quite sure just what, but the Minister of Militia will explain the whole matter when his estimates are under consideration. My impression is that the chief censor there gets $8 a day, and the two assistants $7 a day.
I have been told that they get $10 a day, and that each one rests about three days a week, but the pay goes, on just the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think the chief censor gets $8, and the two assistants $7.

If the services of these gentlemen are necessary, I have no objection at all to their employment. Indeed I shall be very glad to see them employed. But there is an impression, which I should be glad to know can be dispelled, that the services of these three gentlemen are not necessary. Personally, I do not know. Perhaps we can get the information from the Minister of Militia.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He will be here when his estimates are up.
But he is so busy that one hates to bother him. I would sooner bother the Minister of Marine. This thing is in his own constituency, and I have no doubt he recommended these gentlemen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, I was asked to recommend three.

And imy hon. friend
gave no thought to the question whether they were really required or %not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I supposed the Militia Department would not ask for them if their services were not required.

I am glad my hon.
friend has such confidence in the Militia Department. It is said my hon, friend was acting Minister of Militia at one time; perhaps these men were appointed then.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
They were appointed by the Minister of Militia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Are all the censors in Canada under the direction of the Militia Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I tiiink so.
In regard to the signal office in Halifax; I think my hon. friend said that daily reports were published.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think there is a signal office in Halifax. Halifax gets its signal reports from St. John. I have the list of signal stations here, and Halifax is not included. I might read part of the list: Bersimis, North Sydney, N.S., Lurcher Lightship, Brier island, Pt. Lepreaux, Partridge island, St. John, N.B., Bay St. Lawrence, Money Point, C.B., Flat Point, N.S., Cape Ray, Newfoundland, Chatham, N.B., Pt. Escumiac, N.B., and so on.
What I had in mind was the daily publication of movements of vessels. I thought my hon. friend said that these were published by St. John, Quebec, and Halifax. -

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. Montreal, Quebec and St. John publish daily bulletins, and they are sent over from St. John to Halifax, I understand.
Are they published in Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are immediately telephoned to all interested parties in Halifax.
I was not in when the minister was describing the signal service. What is it, just in a word?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It collects and distributes movements of vessels on the Great Lakes, on the Atlantic, and on the St. Lawrence, and gives the ice and weather conditions generally.
What does the publication consist of; is it posted in shipping offices?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They post up a bulletin.
Administration of pilotage and maintenance and repairs of steamer Eureka, $56,300.
I notice that this item includes repairs to the steamer Eureka, and I see that by Item 256, $100,000 is required to provide a vessel to replace the Eureka. Is the Eureka still in service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes; she is used by the pilot service at Father Point. Both in the report of the Pilot Commission, which was laid on the table of the House last session and in the report of the Lord Mersey Commission appointed to inquire into the Empress 80
of Ireland disaster, it was recommended that a different system of picking up and dropping pilots, although the accident did not occur in consequence of the present system, be adopted. It was recommended that the pilots should board the ships at a different point from where they were dropped so as to avoid the danger of ships crossing one another when coming in towards the shore to pick up or drop the pilot. We have a boat at present there, the Eureka. It is an old boat but apart from that it has not the necessary accommodation and Parliament has made an appropriation for a new boat. We hope to be. able to purchase a boat that is suitable, but if we cannot ' purchase one then we will have to build one.
Are the pilotage commissioners at the ports of Sydney and North Sydney paid out of this fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
They maintain themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are paid out of the
fees they collect at the port of Sydney.
I do not mean the pilots; I mean the commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not know whether
the pilot commissioners are paid anything at all, speaking simply from memory. At many ports the pilotage commissioners receive nothing for their services, but if they are paid they will be paid out of the fees collected at the ports.
The department appoint these commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

I want to say a few
words about the conduct of the commissioners at the ports of Sydney and North Sydney. A couple of years ago they undertook to dismiss men who had grown up in that service. I am not blaming the minister at all; he does not pay them, although he appoints them. But in the interest of the department, and in the interest of the pilotage system, at these ports I would like to draw his attention to the fact that the pilotage commissioners are doing a grievous wrong. Old men who have grown up in the pilotage system, who have been earning their living in that way were dismissed and new men were appointed. The commissioners undertook to dismiss several of these men who had no other occupation and wlv.



were making a success of their work. Four men, including Mr. McGillivray at Low Point, were dismissed without any reason whatever. Under the by-laws of the commission they should have had an investigation in order to find some reason for dismissing these pilots. I am not finding fault with the gentlemen they put in their places. Mr. McGillivray took action against the pilotage commission for wrongful dismissal, the case was heard before one of the very best judges in Sydney and he decided that the commissioners were wrong in dismiss-tins man. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, Mr. McGillivray lost and it is now on appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. I would suggest to the minister that if the department does not pay these commissioners, they are under the jurisdiction of the department by reason of the fact that they receive their appointment from the department and it is therefore incumbent upon the minister to inquire into their conduct. I beg to inform him that in dismissing these men they were doing something which was not in accordance with the faithful performance of their duty. The men whom they dismissed have been practically since that time out of employment. One of them does not need employment because he has other business, but it is very unfair and very unwise to allow these commissioners to indulge in that sort of frivolity because 1 can think of no other word to characterize their action. If they had anything against these men, if there had been an investigation under the regulations and it was found that they were wanting in any respect, I could understand why they should be dismissed. If the minister cannot remedy the wrongs that have -been done there he should see that in future no such wrongs are committed again. To show that the pilotage commissioners knew that they were wrong I may state that The moment D p.m. Mr. McGillivray brought his action against them, and he had to bring action against the commissioners personally, they put him to work and he has been at work ever since.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is the suit still going on?

The suit is still going on and it has been carried to the Supreme Court of Canada. I suppose that if the other three men had had sufficient money to start action that they would have had their jobs back by this time. I do not desire to criticise the minister, bi t I want to

bring this to his attention and the attention of his department.

I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Marine to a very similar case which has occurred in the town of Sackville. The chairman of the pilotage commission there was an old sea captain who had seen service for a long while, and there was a gentleman in that locality who desired to be appointed a pilot. I do not know whether there is an examination which applicants have to undergo for the position, hut at any rate the Board of Pilotage Commissioners would not appoint this man as a pilot. This was going on for two or three years; the minister may remember that there was some correspondence in regard to it. Recently the chairman of the board was dismissed because he would not appoint the man in question a. pilot. He claimed that he was absolutely unfit for the position. Another retired sea captain in that same port was offered the position of chairman of the commission but he refused to take it, because he would not pass this applicant as a pilot. (Since that time still another gentleman has been appointed chairman of the board who is not a seafaring man at all, although he is a very estimable man and I have nothing to say against him. I do not know whether this applicant has been appointed or not . There has been some correspondence within the last four or five months with regard to the subject. I do not know whether -this affair was conducted [DOT]as a matter of patronage or whether it was simply done by the Board of Pilot Commissioners. I shall have no hesitation in giving the minister the names of these gentlemen privately if he wants to look into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We always accept the recommendations of the commissioners before licensing the pilots. I have no recollection of the matter that the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Oopp) refers to. I am sorry we have not the file here to-night, but I will look into it.

Captain - Anderson was the
chairman of the Pilotage Commissioners who refused to appoint this man as a pilot and who, in consequence, was dismissed. The position was offered to another gentleman, Captain Atkinson, who refused to accept it on the condition that he should appoint this man a pilot.

I feel like asking the minister to request the commission at Sydney to give their reasons to the department

for dismissing these men. They had no reasons, there was no investigation, and under these circumstances I think the men should get their positions back.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will look into it.
Maintenance and repairs to wharves, $10,000.
What is that for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is for the maintenance of wharves that are under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The hon. gentleman knows that when these wharves are built by the Department of Public Works they are handed over to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, who manage them and appoint a wharfinger who collects the tolls and so on. There is a provision that repairs not exceeding $50 shall be made by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. If they go beyond that amount the Department of Public Works are called upon to provide for them. It is for that service.
To provide for breaking ice in Thunder Bay and Lake Superior and other points deemed advisable for the good of navigation, $40,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There was a contract for
the breaking of ice in Thunder bay with the Canadian Towing and Wrecking Company which expired last spring. Public tenders were invited for renewing the service and only one tender was received, that of the Canadian Towing and Wrecking Company for $30,000. A new contract has been made at that figure. The contract formerly was for $33,000. Three years ago, when it expired, we asked for-public tenders and there was some competition and a contract was entered into for a sum which was less than $20,000, When that contract expired the contractor was not willing to go on, and we asked for tenders again and this was the lowest and only tender that we received. Included in this estimate there is $500 for the winter ferry service between the mainland and St. Joseph island which is under contract. Then $300 is allowed for keeping open the St. Croix river between New Brunswick and the state of Maine. I believe a similar amount is allowed by the government of the United States, or of the State of Maine, so that the river may be kept open and free from ice.

Is this not rather a broad way to put down an expenditure of $40,000:
To provide for breaking ice in Thunder bay and lake Superior and other points deemed advisable for the good of navigation, $40,000?
80i
That leaves it absolutely for the minister to say what other points shall be taken into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: You cannot foresee whether ice will have to be broken or not, and where you may have to break it. I remember that one year we had a contract with Mr. Playfair, and ice had to be broken on some harbours in the lakes so as to facilitate the grain coming down. Another year, owing to strong representations from those engaged in the grain trade, we had to do ice-breaking on the St. Mary's river or else a good deal of damage would have resulted.

Of course, a good many thousand dollars may be spent on work like this which might not be necessary.
Lighthouse and coast service-repairs to Maritime Road, $1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I suppose some' gentlemen will wonder what a maritime road is, as I have often wondered. In the seventies, the Government of Canada extended the telegraph line along the whole north coast of the Gaspe peninsula, and later to the island of Anticosti, as an aid to shipping, with the satisfactory result that shipwrecks on the island of Anticosti showed an immediate and substantial decrease in number. The north shore of the Gaspe peninsula is very mountainous and rugged and sparsely settled. A road was necessary for the maintenance of^the Government telegraph lines, if for no other purpose, and 185 miles of such road was built. Since then the Dominion Government has regularly contributed towards its repair. The municipalities would only repair the road within their own boundaries, and the Provincial Government would only repair those sections where there was population. There are long stretches of the road without any settlers fronting on it, and in these parts the road became impassable. Dr. Wake-ham, the Superintendent of Fisheries, who has charge of the repairs, recommends that this grant be continued for some years to come, and the Chief Engineer of the Department concurs in the recommendation.
Lighthouse and coast service-to provide for telephones at different points throughout the Dominion in connection with aids to navigation, $5,000.

Where are those
telephones?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not the information at hand just now, but I will furnish a list to my hon. friend.

The minister might
bring it down when next [DOT] he goes into Supply, and give the information to the House, because I wish to have it on Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Very well.
Lighthouse and coast service-for construction of a steamer to replace the Scout, $17,640.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A vote of $90,000 was passed in 1914-15 for a new boat called the Grenville to replace the Scout which was engaged in the buoy service on the St. Lawrence between Kingston and Cornwall. The Scout which was a very old boat was condemned by the inspector, and in the meantime we have chartered a boat for this service. The Grenville was built under contract with Poison's of Toronto and the contract price was $173,389. In 191314, $23,000 was paid and there is $90,000 voted for the present fiscal year 1914-15 leaving a balance due of $55,598. As the Poison Iron v.orks expect to be paid ninety per cent of the contract price before the end of the present fiscal year, it will be necessary to provide for $43,000 in the Supplementary Estimates for 1914-15. The Scout was an old wooden vessel built in Ontario. The Grenville is 164 feet long and 30 feet wide and will be completed for the season of navigation 1915-16.
Lighthouse and coast service-new vessel to replace the Maisonneuve, $30,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Maisonneuve which
was engaged in the light service on the Ottawa river and the Kideau canal was an old wooden boat built at Smiths Falls, and she has been condemned as unsafe. The steamer to replace the Maisonneuve is being built at the Government shipyards in Sorel and is estimated to cost $40,000. A tug called the Maggie May has been chartered at $9 a day to take the place of the Maisonneuve..

What about the Scout?
I saw the Scout last summer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Scout was out last
summer, but she is not fit to go out again.
She did not look so unfit last summer that she could not go out again. I thought she was quite a boat.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As a matter of fact, we have been running her longer than we should have done. She was condemned some years ago.

Surely some use could
be made of her.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think so. She has been condemned by the inspector of boilers and also by the inspector of hulls.
Lighthouse and coast service-amount required to provide a vessel to replace the Eureka, $100,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is what I told the
House about a few moments ago in regard to the pilot service at Father Point. We hope to be able to buy a suitable vessel for a smaller amount than the amount in the estimate, so that we can get it into service during this year. If we proceed to build a new vessel, I am afraid that it will cost more than $100,000. We are looking out now for a suitable vessel.

This $100,000 is put in
simply for the purpose of having it there in case you can find a suitable boat that you can buy at that figure?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will buy one out of this appropriation.
Why bother about buying a vessel this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Because we want it for this season's business on the St. Lawrence. It is only a few months before navigation will open on the St. Lawrence, and if we are to carry out the recommendations made by the Pilot Commission and also by Lord Mersey, we must have a boat as soon as possible. If we have to get the designs and plans made for a boat and ask for tenders and award a contract, we cannot get a new boat until next year and perhaps not then. We are anxious to get a boat as soon as possible to carry out the recommendations.
Amount required to pay compassionate allowance to the widow of second officer Lachance of the C.G.S. Montmagny, who was lost on the occasion of the sinking of that vessel.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is the compassionate allowance to the widow of second officer Lachance of the Montmagny, who was drowned while attempting to rescue passengers when the Montmagny collided with another vessel in the river St. Lawrence off Crane island in September, 1914. He was in the employ of the Government at the time, and it was thought fair to give this compassionate allowance.
Meteorological service, including magnetic observatory-grants, of $500 each to Kingston and Montreal observatories; also allowance of $400 to L. F. Gorman, observer at Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen will see that the estimate is somewhat lower than it was last year. This is due to the fact

that last year [DOT]contained $8,000 for the completion of the observatory at St. John, $5,000 for an observatory at Victoria, and an item of $14,000 for director's residence at Toronto, which has been cut out. Otherwise the items are practically the same as last year. The service is carried on under the direction of Mr. Stupart, the chief of the service, and his headquarters are in the city of Toronto where the observatory is and he has observers in all parts of Canada.
Marine hospitals, including grants to institutions assisting sailors, $75,000.
Is there any change made in reference to the Marine hospital at Bunker's island?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Last year it was contemplated that the hospital be closed there and the seamen taken to the general hospital at the town of Yarmouth.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Nothing further has been done about, the matter.
Wrecked and distressed seamen, $3,000.
What amount was expended last year?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In 1913-14, $1,331.09. Up
to the 31st December of this year, $215. That is for assisting seamen, who are shipwrecked and distressed in foreign countries, to return home.
That policy was introduced only recently?	-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, it is a very old practice.
It is a good one and is to he commended. I did not know it was introduced 'before.

In reference to marine hospitals, take ports where there is not such a hospital. Have the sailors the right to be sent to the nearest hospital to receive aid from the Government and to be looked after?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
We used to have an old hospital at Westcock that has been abandoned. I did not know how the sailors would be treated.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We send them now to the local hospital at Moncton.

Can the minister tell me what amounts have been paid
to the medical men at Chetieamp in the county of Inverness for attending sick mariners last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can give the hon. gentleman that information from the Auditor General's report. For attendance and medicine, Dr. P. J. Fiset was paid $110.75, and Dr. W. LeBlanc, $274; total, less $1 underpaid Dr. Fiset, $383.75.

I suggest to the minister that an improvement might be effected in the work which is being done at Chetieamp by appointing one of these gentlemen at the usual salary. It is customary in other places to appoint one man at a salary of say $300. The whole responsibility would then be upon him, and the results would be more satisfactory. I respectfully ask the minister to take that suggestion into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The salaries in the different places range from $100 to $500, so far as my recollection goes. Perhaps it would be better to arrange to pay the amount in a lump sum. In this case the doctor furnishes his own medicines.
What is paid to the marine doctor at Arichat, N.S.?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Dr. LeBlanc's salary as medical officer is $300.
What is the salary of the doctor at St. Peter's ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Dr. McDonald, $250.

I understood when I was home two or three weeks ago that negotiations have been had between the local hospital board in Piotou and the department with reference to the taking over of the old Sick Mariners' hospital. How does this matter stand ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think the negotiations are almost concluded. We were willing to hand the hospital over to the local hospital board at a nominal rental of $1, subject to certain conditions with respect to repairs, and so on; I have not the details in my mind. There was some little apprehension on their part that after taking the hospital and 'Spending some money on it we might probably take it back. There is not the slightest danger of that, however, because the idea of having marine hospitals has practically been abandoned. In every place where there is a proper public hospital the Marine Department makes arrangements with the hospital trustees to take all sick seamen at certain.

per diem rates. We find that this arrangement is better for the seamen, because they get better accommodation, and the cost to the department is very much less.

The organization
which conducted the negotiations with the minister in this matter was a local hospital board composed of persons of all denominations who are interested in charitable work. They did entertain an apprehension along the line suggested by the minister, and I pointed out to them that, from what I knew of the subject, the general policy of the department was primarily to see that the sailors were properly cared for, and that so long as the conditions of the transfer were carried out, the department would not take the hospital from them. I thought that the conditions proposed by the minister were fairly reasonable, and I said so. I hope the matter will be carried through, because the local people will be able to do the work very well.
If an arrangement is made to send sick mariners to a local hospital, is the salary to the medical health officer continued?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. I will not say that there may not be exceptions to that rule. In a case where a hospital has been but recently taken over, the salary may continue for a short time, but the rule is that when a hospital is taken over the salary to the port physician ceases, because there is nothing for him to do.
Steamboat inspection, $83,265.
1 Mr. NESBITT: What was the cost of this service last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is one of the few items in respect of which there is an increase. Inspectors' salaries will amount to $55,800, allowing for increases for the present inspectors and for salaries for other new inspectors whom it is necessary to appoint. One additional inspector has been appointed in Edmonton. The importance of this was urged upon me by the hon. member for Edmonton. There was no inspection of hulls in that district, and, as an inspector had to be sent a distance to make inspections there, a great deal of inconvenience resulted. The new inspector in that district is Mr. J. D. Matthews. The department has been giving some consideration to the necessity of appointing a hull inspector at Vancouver, where there is none at present. The remaining amendment is to cover travelling expenses and so on. This

includes travelling expenses of the inspectors, Mr. Ferguson, who is chief inspector, Mr. Duguid, naval architect, and Mr. McDonald, together with the travelling expenses of customs officers who from time to time assist us in this work. Salaries and inspectors, $48,850; travelling expenses of inspectors at $50 a month, 25 men, $15,000; Mr. Ferguson, estimated, $800; Mr. Duguid, estimated, $1,000; Mr. McDonald, estimated, $100; customs officers, $250. Adding 5 per cent for legal and other incidental expenses, we have the total of $83,265. The increases are in consequence of the addition of a new inspection district at Edmonton, and the appointment of an inspector at the port of Vancouver.
What salary does the inspector at Edmonton receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He was appointed at a salary of $1,500 and travelling expenses.
Does his district extend up the McKenzie river?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, it takes in the Great Slave lake district.
Salaries and disbursements of fishery officers, including' the expenses of the Fisheries Advisory Board, and an allowance of $300 to W. J. E. Casey, secretary thereof, $305,000.
I would suggest to the minister the advisability of postponing consideration of the fishery Estimates, as the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) is not here.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We might pass some of
these items on the understanding that when these Estimates come up again any question respecting fisheries can then be discussed.
The increase here of $15,000 is due mainly to the fact that we expect to take over the administration of the fisheries in the tidal waters of Quebec west of Point Des Monts. It may be that we shall not take them over this year. The question of control of fisheries in tidal waters has been a vexed question for years. We made an arrangement, pending a legal decision, by which we would take control west of Point Des Monts. The case was referred to the Privy Council by a case agreed upon by the Dominion of Canada and the Government of British Columbia, and most of the other provinces intervened. Judgment was given by the Supreme Court of Canada; the case went to the Privy Council and the judgment there was in favour of the contention of the Federal government that there was a public right of fisheries

in the tidal waters and there being a public right of fisheries control was in the Federal Parliament. That is disputed by the province of Quebec. The province of Quebec claims that it is in a different position from the other provinces, that Magna Charta, under which this right of fisheries exists, does not apply and is not in force in Quebec. We gave notice that we would administer the fisheries and issue licenses; Quebec has done the same thing. We have had correspondence with Quebec and have suggested that, as apparently they are acting^ in good faith and we are acting in good faith another case should be taken for the consideration of the Supreme Court of Canada and then for the Privy Council. They have not agreed to that. Negotiations or correspondence is taking place now between the Minister of Justice of Canada and the Attorney General of Quebec, and I think some arrangement will probably b'e come to under which the question will be brought before the court for final settlement. It may therefore be that for the coming season we shall not attempt to enforce our rights but shall let 'matters remain in statu quo.
Are these fishery officers in all cases the persons who collect the claims for fishing bounties and pay out the bounties to fishermen?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In nearly all cases they
are.

Referring to a return laid
on the table of the House with reference to a motion of mine as to tire salary paid to Ward Fisher, Inspector of Fisheries in Shelburne, I find that in 1912 his disbursements were $338.40. That is for six months. But in 1913 they went up to the magnificent sum of $1,009.84. Have the department any control over the disbursements or can the inspector charge what he desires? It looks to me as if $1,009 for one year was a very large sum indeed. In addition to that he charges expenses in coming to Ottawa to	assist the Shellfish Commission $113.70. He must have come up in a private car and gone back in the same way to run up such a bill coming from Shelburne here. In addition to that he paid a stenographer $58, which made $2,384.76 for one year. I say that amount is ridiculous and absurd, and it is taking money out of the pockets of the people, to which this gentleman is not entitled. Disbursements are larger than they have ever before been for the occupant of this office. The Government, in their kindness of heart
and from the fulness of the treasury, are paying this man in war time double the salary paid to his predecessor. I think it is time this gentleman came down to a salary such as others in the country have to live on.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Ward Fisher is, I am informed, a very competent and first-class man, and is doing first-class work. I do not think I ever met him personally, but I am told he is giving full return for every dollar he is receiving. Of course, an inspector who does not inspect is no good, and an inspector 'who does not travel about cannot do very much. An energetic man who gives the necessary time to his duties will have a larger. expense account than a man who performs his duties in a per-lunctory way. All accounts have to be accompanied by vouchers, for instance, a man furnishes vouchers for his hotel bills. When the accounts are furnished they are gone over by the accountant of the department, checke'd up and verified before being paid. As to the bill of expenses coming to Ottawa, he came here at the request of the Shellfish Commission and they kept him here for a considerable length of time. The vouchers for travelling expenses would all pass under the eye of the accountant, and would not be passed unless they were correct. When the return for which my hon. friend has moved comes down, and we are getting it ready, he will be able to get the information more in detail than I can give him.
Why does the inspector need a stenographer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He has a very large amount of correspondence, especially with his department, and has a great many reports to make on license and other matters. I do not think it is unfair to allow him a moderate sum for a stenographer. The salary he receives himself is only $1,300, which in this age and generation is not a large salary for a competent man filling an important position.
Do they all get the same allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It varies with the work of the district. The fishery inspector on the river St. John gets $700, I think; and Mr. Morrison, the fishery inspector for northern New Brunswick, including the counties of Restigouche, Gloucester, Northumberland, Kent, Westmorland and Albert, gets $2,000, but no allowance for a stenographer. I
.COMMONS
think that is by long odds the heaviest district in the maritime provinces.
I understand then that he is getting $100 more than was put down in the answer to this question?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a schedule of wages. The inspectors start at a certain figure and get a yearly increase of $100 up to $1,500, which is the maximum; so that extra $100 is accounted for by the yearly increase.

He started with $600 more than the old inspector, and he gets an increase of $100 a year up to $1,500. His salary then in a few years will be two and a half times more than the salary of any other inspector.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My fishery officers tell me that it was the old inspector's fault. Before I came into office he was suspended for not attending to his duties. He would not carry out his instructions or do his work. He was getting all he was worth and more.
You would not expect him to do for $600 what another man would do for $1,200. This gentleman with double the salary can afford to do the work very much better.
Do all fishery inspectors get an allowance for a stenographer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They all get an allowance
except Mr. Donald Morrison, and I think Mr. Harrison.
Is there an allowance in Cape Breton? -

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

I am afraid Mr. Morrison
will be asking for an allowance now for a stenographer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, I am afraid this discussion will put him on the qui vive.

He is on the right side of
politics, and will no doubt get one.
He is getting about the highest salary of them all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He has the largest district in the maritime provinces, and devotes his whole time to it.
I presume that he has under him a large number of what .we call local inspectors?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Overseers, they are all included in this.
As I understand it, the overseers in my district get a salary of $150.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The pay is very small.

And they are allowed so
much for travelling expenses. I would suggest to the minister that it might be better to give them a bigger salary, and cut out the travelling expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is this about it. If you pay an inspector a lump salary there is no incentive for that man to travel around and. see that the regulations are being enforced in different parts of, the district, whereas if he is allowed a reasonable compensation for travelling expenses he is much more likely to see that the work is properly done.
I know my own district very well, and it is very easy down there to drive 20 miles in order to reach a place only 10 miles distant.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They ought to play the
game. -

I do not say they do that,
but it might be done.
Can the minister inform us as to the increases in salaries of fishery officers since 1911?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Inspector Calder is in charge of the Charlottetown officials and of the eastern part of St. John county and of the Isles of Grand Manan. He was getting $1,100 in 1911, and has had a yearly increase of $100 since, so that brings him up to about $1,400 this coming year; the same applies to Mr. Matheson of Charlottetown. Mr. Harrison, whose district is a small one, is getting the same pay as in 1911, $700.

Unfortunately he is not a
supporter of the present Government. That accounts for the fact that the fairy godmother has not visited him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Let me say that Mr. Harrison was a candidate against me on two occasions in the county of Sunbury. On one of those occasions he was fishery inspector and resigned his office to run against me, but immediately he was defeated he was reappointed fishery inspector.
That was a great many years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think I have shown very much revenge considering that he is still a fishery officer. I do not think that my hon. friend would suggest that he has
[Mr. Hazen.J

not been treated with a fair degree of consideration.
Was not that in local politics, and was not one of the most prominent members of my hon. friend's Government a prominent Liberal, and was not that Administration alleged to be a coalition government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What has that got to do with the fact that he ran against me?

It would afford no excuse for my hon. friend, when he comes to Ottawa as Minister of Marine and Fisheries in a Conservative Government, to dismiss Mr. Harrison because he ran in a provincial election.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will only quote the words of my hon. friend's leader, who laid it down as a principle, that if a man took an active part in either Dominion or local politics, he could not find fault if he was removed from office. It was on that occasion that my- right hon. friend said: "We feel that if a man wants to be a politician we ought to give him every opportunity to be one."
He is a good man at any rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Oh, I think he is perhaps
a fairly good man. To return to the fishery inspectors. Mr. Hockin, who has been inspector in Pictou a great many years, was getting either $900 or $1,000 in 1911, and is now getting $1,300.
What about Mr. MacLeod of Cape Breton?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. MacLeod is now getting $1,300, so my hon. friend will see the salaries are pretty uniform.
Are these increases provided by statute or by the recommendation of the department ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There has been an Order in Council passed providing for the increases. I found it .almost unbearable to have people getting their friends to write in order to get increases in their salaries and .so on. I felt that there should be some principle, or method, that would be uniform, and I got an Order in Council passed. providing that these men should get an increase of $100 a year up to $1,500.
What salary does Mr. Wood get in the northern. Alberta district ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Wood is a fishery overseer, not a fishery inspector; he gets $500.
Has there been any increase in 'the salaries of fishery overseers in Nova Scotia in the last two years ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In western Nova Scotia there was a reorganization last year. We gave the overseers more pay, with no allowances.
What are the salaries at present ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In Annapolis county, W. Purdy, Deep Brook, $700;' Digby, W. Aymar, $500; G. E. Torrie, $700; Kings county, E. F. Reid, $200; Lunenburg, A. J. Evans, $200; Queens county, Charles Young, $700; Shelburne county, George Walls, $750; Yarmouth county, J. B. d'Entremont, $800.
I did not hear the minister name the officers in Richmond.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Western Nova Scotia is where we have had the reorganization. We hope to follow that up with a further reorganization in other parts of Nova Scotia.
Do the fishery overseers in eastern Nova Scotia remain as they were ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
I would like to know about the fishery guardians.
What are the duties of one Cameron who was appointed to assist Mr. McLellan in Inverness county ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think he is a fishery guardian.

I understand that
Cameron is doing a part of the work that Mr. McLellan used to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Guardians' duties are to assist the overseers.

But these are not
guardians.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Cameron is a guardian.
Where does he operate?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have a list of overseers in Nova Scotia, and I have a list of overseers in Inverness county, and Cameron's name does not appear among them; so that if he is a fishery officer, he must be a guardian.
That is what I want to find out. It appears that McLellan was the overseer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: McLellan is the overseer.
Yea, John B. McLel-lan. I understand that some of Mr. Mc-Lellan's duties were taken away from him and that Mr. Cameron was appointed to do this work.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I should not think that very much of his duties would be taken away from him, because I see that he only gets $50 a year.
That is at present, but what was it before the change was made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think it is the same. Cameron is not an overseer. His name does not appear in the list, and therefore he must be a fishery guardian.
Cameron is doing some of McLellan's work; he is not a guardian.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: From the information I have before me I am satisfied that he is not an overseer. I have not the list of guardians here, but if my hon. friend will come to my department and see Mr. Found, he will get all the information.
Has the minister the list of guardians in Yarmouth county?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No; I have not the guardians; I have the overseers.

Would the minister
kindly give the salaries of the overseers in Gloucester county?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Gloucester county: Edmund Arseneau, Inkerman, $140; E. Sewell, Poke-mouche, $140; Thomas Canty, Bathurst, $200; J. P. Doucet, Petit Rocher, $200.
Will the minister be good enough to let me have a list of the overseers in the county of Richmond before the items come up in committee again?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, I will have one sent to the hon. gentleman.
And of Yarmouth, too?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Will this be a list for the coming year or for last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As it is at the present time.
Does the department make it imperative for the overseers to send in the names of the guardians early in the season, or is there any fixed time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The same method is* now adopted as that which has been in force almost since the department began.
They are appointed annually?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

If the Minister has a list of guardians for Inverness
10 p.m. county for the year 1915, will he be good enough to send it to me?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, as soon as it is completed I will send it to my hon. friend.
What salary is Mr. Chapman getting?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Chapman is getting $709 a year.
I understand that is his retiring allowance.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not a retiring allowance; he is acting in an advisory capacity.
What was his regular salary before that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: And the present incumbent is getting $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Chapman was advanced in years, and I had him appointed at $700 a year in an advisory capacity. I think my hon. friend approved of it.
Would the minister send me a list of the guardians in Halifax county?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
Building- fishways and clearing rivers, $30,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In 1913-14 the expenditures under this item were $12,341. In 1914-15, up to December 31, they were $8,837. The largest expenditures are usually in British Columbia where, owing to the nature of the country, jams form in the important fishery rivers from time to time which have to be removed, frequently at considerable expense. The natural obstructions, such as falls, may sometimes be removed, affording access for the fish to important spawning grounds.
Canadian Fisheries Museum, $8,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I wish hon. gentjemen
who are interested in fisheries would, if they have not already done so, visit the Museum, as I believe there is something to interest them there.
There is a reduction of $8,000 in this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have been getting the Museum established for some years, and now we are clear of that expense, so that we can reduce the rate by one-half.
What officials are employed there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is Mr. Halkett, who is a scientist and a man of high standing as a biologist, and1 there are also Mr. Rochon, Mr. Grignon and Mr. Rice.
Oyster culture, $6,000.
What is this for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The department has had for some years the services of Mr. Kemp, who is an expert in oyster culture, and during the present year much of the time has been spent in endeavouring to rid the beds in Richmond bay, Prince Edward Island, of star-fish. Mr. Kemp also gives advice and instruction to those who are taking up oyster culture. In view of the uncertainty as to the ownership of the -barren bottoms suitable for oyster culture, for . many years after the Privy Council's decision nothing was done as neither the Federal nor the Provincial Government felt in a position to grant leases of these areas. Following our amendment to the Fisheries Act in 1912, agreements were entered into with the provincial governments of the three maritime provinces, and in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick considerable progress has been made in building up an industry in oyster culture and cultivation. The star-fish in Richmond bay are proving a great enemy to the oyster, and as everything has an enemy it is said that the enemy of the star-fish is the lobster, and that the reason the star-fish are doing more harm than formerly is because there are not so many lobsters. Steps are being taken to try to get rid of the star fish in Richmond bay. As my hon. friend (Mr. J. J. Hughes) knows, in his own province and in the counties of Kent, Westmorland the barren bottoms have been planted on quite a large scale, and I think the experiment will be successful as was the case in Rhode Island where the oyster beds were depleted to a great extent and are now being renewed.
This vote is not all for M|r. Kemp's salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. Kemp's salary is less
than $2,000, but he has travelling expenses and the maintenance of a boat has to be provided for.

How is the oyster
bed in Caribou harbour progressing?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think that is being attended by the government of Nova Scotia.
The deputy minister will recall that some four or five years ago the oyster expert of the Dominion Government set out a bed in Caribou harbour; is there any report as to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am informed that five or six years ago there was a bed planted there, and it has been carefully looked after, and is doing very well.	.
I would be obliged if the deputy minister would send me the last report on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That will be done.

Does Mr. Kemp
hire a boat?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, he uses a Government boat called the Ostrea.
To pay customs officers for service in connection with issuing modus vivendi licenses, $900.
Mr. KY'TE: How is this amount appropriated to the different customs officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The modus vivendi license, which amounts to $1.50 per registered ton, is issued by the customs officers, and we pay them a commission of five per cent.

Has'the minister ever taken into consideration the question of reducing the modus vivendi license fee to a nominal sum? I have no definite views upon the matter, but I know that the opinion has been frequently expressed that now inasmuch as Canadian fish have largely free entry into American ports, the modus vivendi license fee should be reduced to a nominal sum. I think it is worth considering, and I would ask the minister if representations have been made to him in respect to this matter. I did not know until lately that the department refuses to issue licenses to American fishing vessels propelled by gasoline. I am informed that it is claimed by the department that the provisions of the Treaty of 1818 preclude the issuing of licenses to that class of fishing craft. I would hardly think it proper to refuse a modus vivendi license to American vessels just because they are propelled by some power other than sail. In some of the southwestern counties of Nova Scotia there is a great deal of opposition to the policy of not issuing licenses to that class of fishing vessels, thus preventing them coming to Nova Scotian ports at a considerable loss to the ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There -are a good many phases of this question that have required
127G
It would be a mistake to repeal the modus vivendi.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. There may be a
change of Government in the United States, and the Republican party may come back to power. They might reimpose the duties on fish going into the United States. While we have the free admission of fish into the United States, our fishing boats cannot take their fish there and sell them. They have

to transfer the fish to some mercantile boats. Take a boat that is going out from Lunenburg or Canso or any town in Nova Scotia, which has a cargo of fish. If she takes the fish to an American port and tries to sell them, she will not be allowed to do so. The fish must be in a vessel engaged in the mercantile business. If an American fisherman comes into one of our ports under the modus vivendi, he is allowed to clear to the shipping grounds. If a Nova Scotia boat goes across to Boston or any other port in the United States and wants to get away, she cannot clear for the fishing grounds; she has first to clear for some port in Canada and them clear from there to the fishing grounds. Therefore we are not on an equal basis with the United States, as we are giving them certain benefits under the modus vivendi which they are not allowing us. Under those circumstances, and in view of the fact that we do not know what the future may hold for us, I do not think it would be well for us to repeal the modus vivendi. There are places in Nova Scotia where years ago the people would have been glad to see the modus vivendi repealed; but they would not like to see it repealed to-day, although they would like to have a nominal fee imposed. This matter requires very careful consideration. Hon. gentlemen know the history of the modus vivendi, how it was expected that the Washington treaty would be confirmed under which we were to get free admission of our fish into .the United States on the condition that we would give the same rights to our ports for United States fishing vessels that were enjoyed by our own people. There was a delay in the Washington treaty being confirmed on account of the general election that was approaching, and therefore the modus Vivendi was passed under which fishing vessels of the United States were allowed, on payment of $1.50 a ton, to come into Canadian ports for the purpose of landing crews and transhipping their fish; whereas without that agreement they had only the privilege under the treaty of 1818 which gave the American vessels the right to come into Canadian ports for four purposes, namely, for wood, shelter, repairs and water, and for no other purpose whatever. Under the modus vivendi they have practically all the privileges of our own fishermen. Different views may be taken' about the question, and I do not think anything should be done in a hurry under present conditions.

At the last general election, some of the hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly from Nova Scotia, raised the issue to which the minister has just referred, namely, the inability of Canadian fishing vessels to proceed from the fishing grounds to United States ports. There may be some disabilities of that nature, but 1 do not think it is a settled matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What I am speaking of is a very recent treasury rule. It was called to my attention within the last two days. We have sent for a copy of it to be certain about the matter.

I would suggest this: if the United States market is of any benefit to Canadian fishermen-and I believe it is -then we should do everything in our power to preserve that market. The continuance of the modus vivendi license may be an irritant to those of the United States interested in the fishing business, and it will be used by American interests antagonistic to the present American tariff upon fish products as a ground upon which to urge a change in the present tariff and a reversion to former high tariff duties. If there is a disability against Canadian fishing vessels reporting to American ports directly from the fishing grounds, the minister should take up this matter with the United States Government and there should be some conferences with them upon that subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The total collections amount to less than $10,000.

It is not very much, but perhaps a reduction might have the effect of causing the United States to maintain their present tariff on fish. As the minister himself suggested, the United States frequently change their tariffs, and it would be a great loss to Canada if the former tariff rates on fish were restored. As to the prohibition against issuing licenses to fishing vessels propelled by gasoline or other power, I am surprised to learn that there is such an Order in Council in existence. I never heard of it until recently. I do not think it is fair; I mink it will operate against our own interests. In counties like Shelburne, Queens, Yarmouth and possibly Iligby, this prohibition, I am informed, means a considerable loss of trade to many of the ports in these counties. If sailing vessels are permitted to obtain a license, it seems most illogical to say that vessels propelled by gasoline cannot obtain a similar
license. One needs only to state the facts to disclose the absurdity of the position.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have had correspondence with the authorities in the United States about this matter, which is really under consideration at the present time. But does my hon. friend think that the question of the American tariff would be very much affected, by our action in regard to modus vivendi?
The fishery interests in Gloucester and Boston are very powerful.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The free admission of fish was a provision of the tariff of the Democratic party, which declared in favour of cheaper food for the people of the United States and for the removal of any imposition by way of tax upon it. I doubt very much whether our making a nominal charge would effect the attitude of the people of the United States; I am inclined to think that they would be guided by what they consider to be their own interests in the matter. If they believe that it would be to the advantage of their people to get our fish without the payment of duty, then they will continue the free fish provision. But if, on the other hand, they should think that the free admission of fish interferes with the interests of American fishermen, the chances are that they would put the duty on again. I doubt very much whether any action on our part in respect of a small matter like the modus vivendi license would affect that larger question.

Does a license
under modus vivendi give the right to land fish and to ship them in bond?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, to land fish and to
ship through Canada to the United States.
To provide for the exhibit of fresh and cured food fish at the Toronto annual exhibition, $15,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The year before last, for
the first time, we got an appropriation for the purpose of making an exhibit of fish at the Toronto exhibition, and the exhibit was so successful that we repeated it last year. The directors awarded us a gold medal for our exhibit; they said it was one of the best at the fair. I think that this exhibit at the Toronto exhibition has done a great deal to give the people an idea of the extent of the Canadian fisheries. Fish dealers in Toronto tell me that as a result of the exhibition of fresh and cured fish at the Toronto fair the demand for fish obtained from the Atlantic and Pacific provinces was very considerably increased. The

directors are most anxious that we should continue the exhibit, and I believe that it is in the interests of the country that we should do so.

How do you
spend $15,000 on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We did not spend that
amount. In the first year we spent $9,700 and since that $7,600. We had the idea last year that we might operate a restaur-rant where people could obtain fresh fish each day. We could not work the idea out, however; it was difficult to get a staff to take charge, and other obstacles presented themselves. I do not know Whether or not we can do it this year, but the larger amount would enable us to carry out that idea. I was at the Toronto exhibition last year for the first tirnie, and I was surprised at its extent; undoubtedly it is the largest annual affair on the continent of America. Each day they have a luncheon, which is attended by several hundred persons and at which addresses are given on various subjects. They have an agricultural day, an educational day and so on; I suggested to the president that they should have a fisl| day. I observe that this year they are announcing a fish day, and at the luncheon addresses will be delivered dealing with our fisheries, the advantage of fish as a food, and so on. nil these things help to make the people understand the value of our Canauian fisheries.
A great deal would depend upon the manner in which the fish is prepared. In Ottawa it is almost impossible to get fish properly prepared.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They do not know what salt fish is.
They certainly do not know how to prepare fish for table use.
Could not that portion of the exhibit which consists of cured fish be preserved from year to year, so that the expenditure under that head would be avoided?
