speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think some of it is being preserved.
Salaries, building and maintenance of fishbreeding establishments, $400,000.
Are lobster hatcheries included in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Has the minister any report from the lobster hatcheries in our province as to whether they are successful or otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We get regular reports from all the hatcheries. There is no question as to the success of the salmon and white-fish hatcheries, but the lobster hatcheries have so far been only in the experimental stage. We believe that some advantage is beginning to result from the operations of these hatcheries; I understand that along the Northumberland straits that is the opinion of the fishermen. I do not believe, however, that the fishery experts have learned as yet the proper method of putting . these lobsters into the water in such manner as to prevent large numbers of them from being destroyed. The Biological Board of Canada is experimenting at the lobster pond at Digby with a view to overcoming this difficulty. Generally speaking, however, I think that results are beginning to show from the lobster hatcheries.
Inspection of canned and pickled fish, $25,000.
Is this to be expended under the Act passed last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Would the minister allow that to stand? It is a new and rather important item, upon which there will be considerable discussion when other hon. gentlemen are present.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We might pass it on the understanding that it may be discussed on another occasion under any other item.
I see that the amount provided in 1914-15 was $50,000, and that the amount for 1915-16 is $25,000. Does that mean that more than $25,000 was spent in -1914-15?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, we spent only about $3,000. We estimated too much last year, the reason being that we took over from the Department of Agriculture the administration of the Meat and Canned Foods Act, so far as it relates to canned fish. At the time the Estimates were prepared last year it was thought it might be necessary to have a separate set of officers to carry out the provisions of that Act, but we found that on the Atlantic coast it would be sufficient to confine the inspection to factories, and the existing staff were able to carry out the inspection. We are getting our inspectors appointed, and some of them have been meeting the fishermen, instructing them about barrels, etc.
Have any officers been appointed in Nova Scotia to carry out the Act ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Some have been appointed. There are six districts for the purpose of this Act. District No. 1 includes t-he Gaspe peninsula and other parts of the Gulf coast of Quebec. No inspector for that district has been appointed. District No. 2 comprises the country from Restigoubhe county to Kent county, inclusive, in New Brunswick. An inspector has been appointed for that district, Mr. Colson Hubbard. District No. 3 comprises Prince Edward island, the Magdalen island and the counties of Pictou, Colchester and Cumberland. No inspector has yet been appointed for that district. District No. 4 comprises Cape Breton island. An inspector has been appointed for that district, Mr. Herbert Mann.
What is the salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: And have they an allowance for travelling Expenses ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Travelling expenses will
be paid. District No. 5 is from Antagonist! to Yarmouth county. Mr. Hilts has been appointed for that district. District No. 6 comprises the Bay of Fundy, counties of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, including Charlotte county, St. John county, Albert county and Westmorland county in New Brunswick, and Pictou and Hants in Nova Scotia. The inspector appointed for that district is Mr. A. O. Havelock Wilson.
How many local inspectors will there be ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There will be only the six district inspectors.
Will there be any other salaried officers to carry out the law ? Will one inspector be able to carry out the inspection for the four counties in Cape Breton ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The inspector will go to any point where he is required to inspect fish and see that they are packed and in proper condition and in proper barrels. If they are, he places the prescribed mark upon them, showing that they are properly packed.
Suppose that half a dozen fishermen at one point wish to have fish inspected one week and the following week half a dozen others in the same place. Would the inspector have to make two visits ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He would have to go back, but we naturally suppose that fishermen
wanting to have fish inspected would try to arrange to have one visit cover them all. Of course we want to do what is convenient for the fishermen.
Is it possible for all fishermen in a district to have their fish ready for inspection at the same time ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These are pickled fish and could wait for a while.
I am afraid the minister will discover after a time that it will be impossible to carry out the intention of the Act with only one inspector for each group.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If more are required, I
suppose we will have to get them, but we are simply starting the system and we will have to feel our way with it. The Act is not compulsory. By the end of another year we shall have a better knowledge of what is required.
I hope the minister is appointing competent inspectors. Who are Mr. Mann and Mr. Hilts, and what are their- occupations?
Mr. Hilts belongs to Mahone bay in Lunenburg county. He has been foreman for a large fishing firm and is an expert in the business.

Who is Mr. Herbert Mann?
Mr._ HAZEN : I have not the recommendations here, but on asking his qualifications we found that they were quite right. The qualifications laid down were that the^ should be healthy, accurate, strictly temperate, and, if possible, not more than 40 years of age; they should possess a reasonably good education, be capable of intelligently imparting instruction to fishermen and packers and have been directly engaged in the fishing business and have special knowledge of the curing of mackerel and herring. The general inspector is to be an expert in fishery matters, and have a knowledge of barrel making. Each inspector gets $1,200. In district No. 2 it was necessary to have an inspector who could speak the two languages. Mr. Havelock Wilson of St. John has been engaged in the fishing business all his life; he is a very intelligent man, of good education, respectable in every way, and with a thorough knowledge of the fishing business. Mr. Colson Hubbard carried on the fishing business in Gloucester county for a number of years, and is also very familiar with all the details of the business, and speaks French as well as English.
Does the minister happen to know where Mr. Mann, the inspector for Cape Breton, lives?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am informed that he is from Sydney.
Sydney would be rather an unexpected place to find a gentleman with these qualifications, because there is no one in the fishing business there.
How many inspectors are there for Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I explained that there is
one inspector for district No. 3, which includes the Island and the counties of Pic-tou, Colchester and Cumberland.

Is that district not too
large?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I think the division of districts is pretty good.

Do you permit
the inspectors to engage in any other occupation?	/

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, we expect them to give all of their time to this work.

I hope that all the appointments made will come up to the standard fixed by the department. I think there should be a very high standard for such officers. These men have the opportunity of doing an educative work among the people whose fishery products they inspect. I think it is desirable that they should be well educated. I hope the minister will see that those who are appointed do not treat their appointment merely as a way of getting a living. They should be interested in their work, because if they are competent men they can do a great service to the State.
To provide for the building of fisheries patrol boats, $32,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is to provide a pew
boat for the Magdalen islands. The Semiahamo, the old patrol boat, has been condemned by the inspector. These boats will be gasoline.
. To provide for a fisheries patrol steamer for Lake Winnipeg, $100,000.
This is a pretty expensive boat.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
-We asked for tenders for the construction of that boat, but not a single firm in Canada tendered. The difficulty was that the boat was for 'nke Winni-

peg, and would have to be assembled out there. As not a single firm tendered, we are building the boat ourselves at Sorel, and it will be sent out there to be assembled. I dn not think the cost is excessive, considering the locality and the difficulties of the situation. The fisheries of lake Winnipeg are getting more and more important all the time, and so is the' general commerce of the lake. There was an old boat there called the Lady of the Lake, but it is now obsolete. Hon. gentlemen may be interested to know that the name of the new boat is the George H. Bradbury.
To provide for an investigation into the fisheries of Hudson bay, $10,000.

Why does not
the minister take that out and relieve the Finance Minister to that extent? It is no good.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member will remember that two years ago there was a discussion in the House as to the necessity of our getting information with regard to the fisheries of Hudson bay. I think my hon. friend from Edmonton is quite interested in the matter. Last year we started to get information, and we had a vote in the Estimates for $15,000, of which we have spent $13,109. We have sent out three expeditions, two of them overland. The two overland expeditions confined their attention to James bay and the tributary waters. The report of each of these expeditions has been published and laid on the table of the House. Not much information has been secured regarding the fisheries of the bay proper, the main attention having been given to the rivers flowing into the bay. There is some reason to believe that valuable fisheries exist in Hudson Bay waters, and we think it wise to continue the investigation.

When I suggested that the amount be struck out I did not know that you were doing any >vork. I think that about two years ago the Government sent a special person to Hudson bay to investigate the fishery resources, but while he drew his salary he never gave ns any information; in fact I do not think he carried on any investigation at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That was Professor
McCarthy, of King's College, Windsor. He had no opportunity of acquiring information considering the conditions.

This amount will enable the Government to complete the investigation?

Department of the Interior-Immigration- Seed grain to settlers on patented and unpatented lands in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta-further amount required, including Governor General's warrants for $3,640,007.20, $8,159,958.25.

It is quite possible that the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) may wish to discuss this. I have no objection to the item going through, provided that my hon. friend agrees to let us discuss it later.

On Monday I am introducing a resolution, upon which a Rill will be founded to legalize the arrangement we have made with various provinces, and any discussion could take place on the resolution or on the Bill.
Or on some other item.
Yes. We are anxious to get this through to-night because many of the lnerchants are waiting to be paid for the relief supplied.
Was any time limit set within which applications for seed grain had to be made?

I gave that information yesterday across the floor of the House in answer to a question from the hon. member for Regina. Applications closed as far as the drouth-stricken area was concerned, on January 31. Applications for the district outside of the drouth-stricken area, but in which the farmers were similarly situated, were received up to February 20. In other portions of the province applications were received up to March 10. That was the last day on which we received applications.

Is that a hard and fast rule? For instance, if a settler in the drouth-stricken area did not know that the distribution closed on January 31, would he be denied the seed if he applied at a later date?

The hon. member will
recognize that we had to fix some date in which applications were to be received; otherwise we should not have known what quantity of grain to purchase, and it takes considerable time to purchase grain and have it put through the elevator, cleaned, bagged, and distributed. We circularized those in the drouth-stricken area, both through the press and by circular, notifying them of the date by which applications had to be in, and I am sure that those within that area had ample time in which to make application; and the best evidence of that 81
is the fact that we have accepted 48,000 applications. Several thousands more have been received, but rejected.

I have a letter making a complaint in regard to another man in connection with this seed grain distribution. This man writes that he had his application accepted for seed grain and that he was afterwards notified by Mr. Bruce Walker that owing to the statement that he did not have eighty acres of land under cultivation he could not be given the necessary grain to seed this land. In the letter which I have before me he states that he has eighty acres of land ready for cultivation. Mr. Walker writes as follows:
Winnipeg-, Man., Feb. 9, 1915.
Sir,-Further to your application for an advance of seed grain, I here notify you that your application for an advance of seed grain has been cancelled as I have been informed that you have not 80 acres under cultivation and that your land is not in fit shape to receive seed.
Kindly destroy the notice sent you that your application had been approved.
(Sgd.) J. Bruce Walker,
Commissioner.
This man had had his application approved by Mr. Walker, and then, on account of Mr. Walker's claiming that his land was apparently not fit for seed, his application was cancelled and he was notified accordingly. I would like to know how Mr. Walker knew that he had not eighty acres under cultivation or that the land which he had under cultivation was not fit to receive seed?
Is this in the drouth-stricken area?
Yes.
You are confident of that?
It is at Bar Hill, Alberta, near Lethbridge.

The only explanation that I can give is that Mr. Walker, or his officials, were instructed to make an investigation in every ease possible and not give seed where the land was not suitable for seeding. We have a great many letters and representations urging us to see that the land is properly prepared for seed and to send out instructors to see that the seed is put in properly. I presume that Mr. Walker had investigated and found out that this man's land was in such a condition that it would be an absolute waste were we to give him the seed. They have been instructed



to investigate as closely as possible in each case.
Has he a special inspector for each case?

He has a number of officials in each district. The drouth-stricken area was divided into five districts almost according to the boundaries of the land districts, and there was a supervisor placed over each one of these districts. He had a certain number of officials to investigate these cases. The Mounted Police are doing a considerable portion of the work at the present time.

There has been a report in the western papers that the seed which is being provided for distribution
11 p.m. is not clear of noxious weeds.
The department is claiming that no land Should be put under cultivation that is not fit. I presume that would mean that unfit land would be full of noxious weeds, and yet the statement is made in the public press that the seed contains a considerable quantity of noxious weeds. The statement may not be absolutely true. Has the department taken any steps to see that the grain has been properly cleaned? [DOT]

Yes, the seed commissioner of the Department of Agriculture is on the ground looking after that. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) has his representative there and it is his special duty to see that seed is sent out containing no noxious weeds. I have never had a single complaint on that score. I believe they were particularly careful in view of the complaints that were received with regard to the distribution of seed in 1908.

In connection with this complaint, the man who wrote this letter from Bar Hill gives the reason why he was refused this grain. The reason may not appeal to the minister. He claims that he is a Liberal, and that the inspector is not of the Liberal faith. There is a personal grudge between these two men and that is the reason why he was refused the grain.
I do not take any stock in that.
You would not believe that?
No, not at all, particularly when Mr. Walker turned down his application.

Mr. Walker would only have the report of his own official in that section. The man makes the statement that the land is in the same condition as that of his neighbours and that his neighbours have been getting the seed while he has been denied it. As regards the quantity of land under cultivation he claims that he has eighty acres. Is there a regulation which requires that there shall be a certain amount of land under cultivation?
There is a maximum quantity of 400 bushels of all kinds of seed grain.
Eighty acres would not require any such amount. Is there a minimum amount of land required to be under cultivation in order to get seed?

Is it possible that he may have asked for more seed than his land would require. If the hon. gentleman thinks he has a complaint that is well founded, let him give me the facts of the case and I will have it specially investigated. If the case is as represented in these letters there is no reason why he should not be supplied with this seed.

Here is Mr. Walker's
statement:
Tour advance has been cancelled as X have been informed that you have not eighty acres under cultivation and that your land is not in fit shape.
It is extraordinary to compel a man to have eighty acres in order to get seed.
It is possible that he may have reported that he had eighty acres ready for seed and it may have been found that this was a misrepresentation. That may have called forth the letter from Mr. Walker.

This man writes that he has twenty acres fall ploughed which he intends to put in wheat and that when he ploughs the rest for oats and flax he will have eighty acres under cultivation in all. The only claim that Mr. Walker can legitimately have against this man is that the land is not fit to receive the seed. The question of the acreage should not enter into the matter at all. If a man asks for seed to sow eighty acres, and if the Government are fully protected by a lien on the man's land, I do not see why Mr. Walker should write telling him that he cannot get the seed. The question is whether this man's land is fit to receive the seed and also whether the inspector of the

department has been fair in stating that the land is not fit for the seed.
Has the hon. gentleman the original letter of Mr. Walker?
Yes.

If the hon. gentleman will hand that letter to me I will have the case investigated.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Hazen the House adjourned at 11.25 p. m.
Monday, March 22, 1915.
